Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/writing-claudinite-skills

# Writing Claudinite skills

A corpus skill is a harness-matched trigger (frontmatter `name` + a tight `description`, plus `force-load-on-file-edits-paths` under `metadata` where an edit of the files it names must not start without it — the PreToolUse guard holds such an edit until the skill is loaded; never the harness's `paths`, which limits when the skill is offered at all) plus the body the agent needs at usage time — well under 500 lines, and nothing a deterministic mechanism could carry instead (the promotion ladder in [engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md) decides). A skill may own the rules that validate its action — `checks.mjs` beside the SKILL.md, one module per rule, with their fixture tests under the owning pack's `test/` mirroring the skill's path; shape and the relevance-first gate in [engine/checks/README.md](../../../../engine/checks/README.md#adding-a-rule). Ownership is placement: the skill lives in exactly one owning pack's `skills/` — there is no skill catalog; the pack's own README names what it bundles. Instruction-writing *quality* — how agents actually follow docs — is [authoring-agent-docs](../../../basics/skills/authoring-agent-docs/SKILL.md)' turf; this skill is the corpus mechanics. (1)

content.content: Launching skill: writing-claudinite-skills

1	---
2	name: writing-tasks
3	description: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.json or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
4	metadata:
5	  force-load-on-file-edits-paths:
6	    - "**/tasks/**"
7	---
8	
9	# Writing a task
10	
11	Every occurrence of every task is an issue in this repo — a `[claudinite-work]` item whose labels
12	are its state — so write the task against that queue, never a runner of its own.
13	
14	**A cadence is one way an occurrence is created, not what a task is.** A task is a
15	unit of the repo's own work with a precondition, a code-work phase and optionally an
16	agentic-work phase; `frequency` says only how often the queue offers to run it, and
17	`manual` — no cadence at all — is a first-class value. Work that fires on an event,
18	on a condition, or on a force is a task in exactly the same sense as work that fires
19	nightly, and reads the same contract. Anything reachable from the executor belongs
20	here rather than in a workflow of its own; see the cron rule below for the narrow
21	case that genuinely cannot be.
22	
23	Three responsibilities, strictly separated (owner, 2026-08-06):
24	
25	1. **The scheduler run** — a vendored hourly Action
26	   (`.github/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml`) that is pure label mechanics
27	   over the issue list: **instantiate** each recurring task's standing item when
28	   its anchor comes, **ready** blocked items whose wait has passed, **reclaim**
29	   dead executor claims. It evaluates no precondition and collects no signal.
30	2. **The executor** — a pull worker over the queue (the scheduler run's post-scheduler run drain,
31	   and a `labeled`-event run for latency) that picks the next ready item, claims
32	   it, evaluates **that one task's** precondition, runs its code-work, and either
33	   converges the item or hands off to an agent session.
34	3. **The task-janitor** — an ordinary daily task (`basics/task-janitor`,
35	   `agent_model: none`) that owns everything about the queue that is *nobody's
36	   task*: items stuck ready past their period, items wearing no state label after
37	   a torn transition, and a health review of the open set.
38	
39	The engine is vendored under `.claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-tasks/`; the basics
40	pack owns the conformance guards for the surfaces a repo authors around it —
41	scheduling is baseline Claudinite discipline, present wherever basics is
42	declared (everywhere), not an opt-in feature.
43	
44	There is no watermark and no per-run state: an occurrence exists because its
45	issue exists, which is why an outage self-heals by looking at the queue rather
46	than by replaying a ledger.
47	
48	## What the checks guard
49	
50	- **The scheduler workflow is a thin shim.** The vendored
51	  `claudinite-scheduler.yml` carries a single **hourly** cron on a repo-hashed
52	  minute constrained to **:10–:50** (the one repo-specific value in the stub —
53	  `packs/claudinite-tasks/hash-minute.mjs`, a pure function of the repo full name that
54	  bootstrap stamps in and baselining re-derives), a `concurrency` group, a
55	  `workflow_dispatch` trigger (whose one `wake` input is how a task is forced,
56	  here or from another repo), and a call into the vendored scheduler run — no logic of its own
57	  (schema and behaviour changes ride the vendor refresh, not workflow edits). It
58	  is the repo's **only** cron; the executor's workflow beside it carries none. Work
59	  that had its own cron'd workflow becomes a **task**, and that workflow is deleted
60	  — its steps move into the task's worker. So does work with no cron at all: an
61	  event-driven or condition-gated job becomes a task on `frequency: 'manual'`, woken
62	  by whatever knows the event happened. Don't keep either as a dispatch-only workflow
63	  for the task to fire: that is two files and two edit sites for one job, and a
64	  workflow whose only caller is the thing that replaced it. (The exception is narrow,
65	  and it is **not** about privilege. An Actions-only secret is reachable from
66	  code-work, which runs Action-side — `code_work_required_secrets`, below. A deploy target's
67	  OIDC identity is one `permissions:` line in the executor's own workflow, not a wall.
68	  A one-shot external effect is handled by `on_interrupt: 'needs-human'`, not by
69	  escaping to a workflow. What genuinely does not fit is the Actions **composition
70	  model**: a `uses:` step is resolved by the runner out of workflow YAML, and code-work
71	  is itself a step's subprocess, so no task — in any language — can invoke one. Work
72	  built on marketplace or composite actions, a Pages deploy being the standing example,
73	  keeps a workflow for those steps. Even then the task owns the trigger and the
74	  decision to run; the workflow carries only the `uses:` steps.) Off-band or multiple
75	  crons, or a missing concurrency/dispatch guard, break staggering, double-run
76	  safety, or manual runs.
77	
78	- **Every declaration carries a `description`** — up to fifty words on what the
79	  task does, or why it exists, for whoever reads the declaration or a roster of
80	  them. It says only what no other field says: never the cadence, the conditions,
81	  the automerge policy, or where the files live — those are read off the fields
82	  beside it, and a description restating them goes stale the day one changes.
83	  `task-declaration-shape` bounds the length; the rest is yours.
84	
85	- **Every task declaration carries the full contract.** A `tasks/<name>/task.json`
86	  (one JSON object, `"$schema"` pointing at `packs/claudinite-tasks/task.schema.json`
87	  so an editor validates it; keys grouped as identity, cadence, outcome, then the
88	  `code_*` fields, then the `agent_*` fields) declares `id` (matching its directory), `description`
89	  (below), `frequency`
90	  (`daily | weekly | monthly | manual`), `expected_outcome` — what the run does to
91	  pull requests, resolved once by the executor before code-work and handed to both
92	  phases: `no_code_changes` (opens none), `fresh_pr` (one on a freshly minted
93	  branch; the task's earlier pull requests are left alone),
94	  `amend_existing_or_create_new_pr` (pushes onto the task's newest open pull
95	  request while it has no conflicts, a fresh branch otherwise), or
96	  `supersede_existing_pr` (a fresh branch, and the task's earlier pull requests
97	  close once its own exists; a green, unlanded one on an auto-merge repo is landed
98	  instead). The retired `none`/`pr` normalize to the first two, and
99	  `open-pr`/`merged-pr` to `fresh_pr` with a policy of `nothing`/`anything`.
100	  Everything else has a default or is conditional: `preconditions` (the conditions
101	  that must hold for it to run — below) is *run always* when absent; `agent_model`
102	  (`opus | sonnet | haiku | none`) is `none`, no agent; `code_work` is no code work.
103	  The two timeouts have **no default**: an agent declares `agent_execution_timeout`
104	  and code work declares `code_work_timeout`, because a running phase always has a
105	  bound. An agent also declares `agent_instructions`, its worker file — nothing
106	  stands in for it. A task whose outcome opens a pull request may also carry
107	  `automerge` — what it authorizes to land unreviewed: `'nothing'` (the default
108	  when absent), `'anything'`, or a list of diff classes, each optionally `reject:`-prefixed.
109	  Choose the **narrowest policy that covers the task's whole write surface** — the
110	  policy is the contract's statement of why landing unattended is safe, and the
111	  policy engine plus the `automerge-policy-scope` check hold every run to it.
112	  **Start from the folder.** A task's write surface is almost always a *place* —
113	  the tree its worker is told to write in, which you know exactly while writing
114	  this declaration — and a folder bound holds where a kind bound does not:
115	  `doc-changes` authorizes Markdown anywhere in the repo, the root `README.md`
116	  included, where `under:<dir>` authorizes one tree and a run that strays parks.
117	  So name the tree inline first, then narrow it by kind where the task writes
118	  only one — **a list is a union, so adding a term widens; `&&` inside a term
119	  narrows**, every part having to match (`under:product-wiki && doc-changes` is
120	  "docs, and only under that folder"). Leave the scope bare where the task
121	  legitimately writes more than one kind: a bare `under:<dir>` covers the code
122	  and the test beside it, where intersecting a code class would park the run the
123	  moment its own test file joined the diff. Reach for a bare kind class only
124	  where the task genuinely writes repo-wide, as a comment sweep does. A pack
125	  declares its own class (a `merge-rules.json` beside its `pack.mjs`) only when a
126	  task knows a finer boundary than a class or a folder can state — a file-name
127	  matcher, or a grant like the mount rewrite's. A `none` task runs no agent, so
128	  `agent_instructions` is not applicable and is omitted. The
129	  scheduler run and executor read agent_model/expected_outcome/frequency from this file — never from the work
130	  item — so an illegal or missing value means a task never fires, fires wrong,
131	  or writes past its declared ceiling. The same contract
132	  (`packs/claudinite-tasks/task-contract.mjs`) is re-validated at run time, so the
133	  static and runtime views can't drift. A task declares **no session scope** — see
134	  the next entry.
135	
136	- **A task's code reads only the environment code-work is handed.** Code-work runs as
137	  a subprocess with a fixed set of `CLAUDINITE_*` variables — `REPO_ROOT`, `REPO`,
138	  `DEFAULT_BRANCH`, `ITEM`, `PACK`, `TASK`, `CONTEXT`, `REQUEST_AGENT`, and the
139	  target's `TARGET_MODE`, `TARGET_BRANCH`, `TARGET_PR` — and
140	  `task-code-work-env` (blocking) rejects a read of anything else. A variable nobody
141	  sets is `undefined`, the parse of it yields empty, and the run goes green having
142	  quietly done something other than what it was asked: that is how three fleet
143	  tasks kept taking their parameters through a channel the queue had stopped
144	  setting, leaving a fleet-wide sweep unable to be scoped or dry-run. **Operator
145	  parameters ride the item's Context** (`CLAUDINITE_CONTEXT`, one line per bullet),
146	  which is the only channel a task may take them from.
147	
148	- **Session scope is retired, and `session_scope` is now inert** (owner ruling,
149	  2026-08-09; the field's last reader went with the slot scheduler). Reach is a
150	  property of **which endpoint the hand-off calls** — `invocation_endpoint`, below
151	  — so a task needing wider access names a different endpoint and nothing else in
152	  the system has a concept of scope. A declaration still carrying `session_scope`
153	  validates and does nothing at all; `task-declaration-shape` raises it as an
154	  advisory rename (advisory on purpose: a member's vendor refresh must not turn its
155	  CI red over a file nothing has edited yet). Drop it, and name an endpoint if the
156	  task actually needed the reach.
157	
158	- **Every run is bounded.** An agentic task (`agent_model !== none`) declares
159	  `agent_execution_timeout` — seconds bounding the agentic run.
160	  There is no platform wall-clock kill for a launched agent session, so the
161	  bound is best-effort: the hand-off surfaces it into the session's brief ("fail
162	  after N minutes") and the agent leash catches a session that never converges its
163	  item. Set it generously — extreme protection against a runaway, not a scheduling
164	  knob. (1)
165	
166	- **A task says which repo secrets it needs.** Code-work runs Action-side, so repo
167	  Actions secrets are reachable there and nowhere else in a task's life (an agent
168	  session carries none). A task lists what it needs in `code_work_required_secrets`
169	  (the retired `required_secrets` still normalizes to it); the
170	  executor holds every repo secret and hands each task's code-work exactly the names
171	  that task declared, so a worker reads it as ordinary environment. A declared
172	  secret the repo has not configured is **named, not guessed at**: code-work is the
173	  only code that sees a secret's value, so the executor parks the item at
174	  `task:status:needs-human-action` saying exactly which one is missing. Nothing else fails; the task
175	  that needs the secret just doesn't work yet. The consequence worth designing
176	  around: **a workflow that exists only to hold a secret is redundant** — fold its
177	  work into the task's code-work rather than dispatching and polling a second
178	  workflow from an agent.
179	
180	- **A standing tracker belongs to the task that keeps one, not to the machinery.**
181	  Nothing in the contract declares a tracker and no task is expected to want one. A
182	  task that keeps an aggregated record across runs resolves the issue in its **own**
183	  code-work and passes the number to its agentic phase the ordinary way — the hand-off
184	  payload's `delivered.issue`, which the executor renders into the work item as an `Issue:` line
185	  the worker doc points at. The exact-title lookup and the create-then-close pair are
186	  a library that code-work may call (`packs/claudinite-tasks/tracker.mjs`), never a phase:
187	  whether a run with nothing to say should mint a tracker at all is the task's own
188	  judgment, and tidy-repo's three answer no.
189	
190	`task-declaration-shape` and `task-md-only-when-agentic` are **relevance-first**:
191	both key off a `tasks/<name>/task.json` existing, so on a repo that carries no tasks
192	they are a no-op.
193	
194	## The task folder
195	
196	One directory per task — `<pack>/tasks/<name>/` — holding **`task.json`** (the
197	declaration, plain data; the retired `task.mjs` module form still loads until the
198	nightly update converts it) beside its worker, plus any deterministic helpers and,
199	where the task's gate is its own, a **`preconditions.mjs`** exporting its terms.
200	The conditions that grant a run also contribute the run's `context` lines, which
201	join the item's own Context as binding constraints the agent may not re-litigate.
202	
203	**The worker is code by default, and the agent is the escalation.** An
204	`agent_model: none` task's worker is a sibling `.mjs` the executor runs as
205	code-work: the item closes on that subprocess's outcome and no session is ever
206	started, which is how a repo runs a deterministic job in Actions without
207	authoring a workflow for it. An agentic task adds **`task.md`**, the spec its
208	session follows, and may still do its own code-work first — escalating the
209	remainder for **work code-work could not do**, never for a re-check of whether
210	the run should have happened.
211	
212	`task.md` is that spec and nothing else, so an agentless task must not carry one
213	(`task-md-only-when-agentic`, blocking): the file's presence is what the rest of
214	the corpus reads as "an agent runs here" — the routine contract judges the folder
215	by it, and every work item names it as the file its run is about. What an
216	agentless task's worker does is documented in a **`README.md`** beside it.
217	
218	**`task.md` describes only what this task must do — never how anything outside it
219	works.** A session opens the file already dispatched, already at its model, already
220	holding its item; restating that machinery teaches it nothing and is read as
221	instruction, so a later run generalizes the description into a rule and acts on it.
222	Keep out how the task is invoked (the executor, the hand-off, the queue's labels),
223	what model it was dispatched at, and what downstream consumes what it produces.
224	Where such a fact carries a constraint the run must obey, state the **constraint**
225	and drop the mechanism: not "you run from a work item the executor handed off whose
226	Context is binding scope", but "the Context section is binding scope"; not "never
227	merge — the executor enforces it in code", but "never merge". The declaration is
228	where the mechanics belong: `agent_model`, `schedule_after` and `expected_outcome` live in
229	`task.json`, and `task.md` never repeats them.
230	
231	This is the task-folder shape of the unattended-agents routine-folder convention; the
232	issue-driven-dispatch security rule (the issue is data, the task path is
233	code-validated, agent_model/expected_outcome come from the repo) lives with that
234	skill's agent practices.
235	
236	### Three optional declarations
237	
238	Declare one only when its rule applies.
239	
240	- **`schedule_after: ['<pack>/<task>']`** — this task yields while a named upstream's item is live
241	  *this cycle*, and picks up the moment it converges. Declare it when your task
242	  reads what another task produces; never as a general priority hint. It is not a
243	  `Blocked-by` edge and must not be described as one.
244	- **`on_interrupt: 'requeue' | 'needs-human'`** (default `requeue`) — declare `'needs-human'`
245	  only for a genuinely one-shot side effect (a store submission, an external notification):
246	  it makes every recovery path that would re-execute the task converge to triage instead.
247	- **`invocation_endpoint: '<name>'`** — a key into the repo's `taskScheduler.endpoints`, for a
248	  task whose agentic phase needs reach the repo's ordinary sessions lack. **Never a URL**: a
249	  task declaration is vendored verbatim into every consuming repo, so deployment detail and
250	  anything adjacent to a credential stay in that repo's own config.
251	
252	One field is **not** yours to declare: `model_from_request`, which lets a task run
253	at the model its ITEM names rather than the one it declares. Exactly one task
254	declares it — the engine's own built-in request implementer, which no pack can be —
255	and every other task names its own `agent_model`.
256	
257	A task's `code_work_timeout` must stay under the executor's one-hour claim leash — a code-work
258	that can outlive it is reclaimed while still running, and the item livelocks. The declaration
259	contract enforces this; do not raise a timeout past it, split the work instead.
260	
261	## Writing `preconditions`
262	
263	**`preconditions` is a list of named conditions, and every one must hold.**
264	`['X', 'Y || Z']` is `X && (Y || Z)`: the comma is `&&`, `||` joins alternatives
265	inside one entry, and a parameterized condition carries its argument inline after
266	a colon (`no-open-pr-touching:product-wiki/`). It is deliberately the opposite of
267	an `automerge` list, which is a union — one field grants, the other requires.
268	
269	```js
270	preconditions: ['substantive-change', 'no-open-pr-titled:Claudinite tidy: improve comments'],
271	```
272	
273	**`['none']` is the empty precondition** — the task runs unconditionally, because
274	its trigger is the calendar or the filed work item itself. It is legal only as the
275	sole entry: any real condition beside it would be the actual precondition.
276	
277	**`preconditions` is the only gate there is.** The `precondition` function and its
278	`precondition_signals` companion are retired: both are rejected by name, and the
279	signal union is derived from the conditions — each names what it reads, so the
280	collector can never disagree with the gate. A gate the built-ins cannot express is
281	a **task-local term** in a `preconditions.mjs` beside the declaration, which is
282	handed `{ arg, config, item, windowDays, now }` and stays pure over them.
283	
284	**Three things are NOT preconditions**, and putting them there is the common
285	mistake:
286	
287	- **Repo shape.** "This repo ships the release pipeline", "this repo has a
288	  vendored mount" are facts adoption settled, not questions worth re-asking every
289	  night. A repo that carries a pack but not one task's subject names that task in
290	  its own `.claudinite-settings.json` — `taskScheduler.disabledTasks:
291	  ['<pack>/<task>']` — which the scheduler reads before instantiating anything.
292	- **Scope.** Which files, PRs or members a granted run works on is the worker's
293	  decision, made in the work sections from the same signals. The conditions decide
294	  run or no-run, nothing else.
295	- **Standing instruction and config** — a `pack_paths` list, a read-only
296	  constraint. Those belong in `task.md`, where they hold on every run.
297	
298	### No task runs on a silent repo unless its declaration says so
299	
300	A repo is *silent* over a window when no substantive commit landed, no issue or PR
301	of its own moved, and no session was captured — **and a scheduled task's own output
302	counts as silence**: a task-authored commit or PR is the machinery running, not the
303	project moving, and a fleet of tasks must not keep each other awake. The delivery
304	lanes stamp `Claudinite-Task: <pack>/<task>` on what they commit and merge, and the
305	movement conditions read it, so this holds for a task added tomorrow with nothing
306	to remember.
307	
308	The vocabulary carries the gate; no operator or marker states it:
309	
310	- **Movement conditions are non-task by construction** — `substantive-change`,
311	  `issues-touched`, `prs-touched` — so a movement-gated task is already
312	  silence-safe.
313	- **A calendar-triggered task that should sleep on a silent repo states
314	  `repo-active`**, the positive umbrella over all four activity dimensions.
315	- **A task whose trigger is not repo movement states its own condition or
316	  `['none']`**, and that absence is visible where a reader audits the trigger.
317	
318	### When no built-in condition fits
319	
320	Ship a **`preconditions.mjs` beside the `task.json`**, exporting `terms`: a map from
321	term name to `{ signals, takesArg?, holds(signals, { arg, config, item }) }`, where
322	`holds` returns `{ holds, reason?, context? }` or `{ error }`. Names resolve
323	against the built-ins first, then the task's own, in one flat namespace where a
324	collision is loud. Reach for it when the gate is genuinely this task's — an age
325	against a configured retention, a manifest against a release tag, a permission
326	check about one named issue — never to re-spell a condition the vocabulary has.
327	
328	A term is handed **this occurrence's own facts** as `item`, for a verdict about one
329	target where the signals describe a window: a request item's verdict is about the
330	issue it names, which no signal bundle can single out.
331	
332	### It fails LOUD, never closed
333	
334	An unknown condition, a malformed argument, or a signal that could not be read
335	returns `{ error }` — a failed run parked in the failure lane, where the re-queue
336	lever retries it — never a decline. A decline is a decision about the world, and
337	one taken on data that was not there is permanent, silent staleness: nothing in the
338	repo goes red when a task quietly stops running.
339	
340	## Which pull request a run works on is the executor's decision
341	
342	A worker never looks for an open pull request, never picks a branch name and never
343	closes a previous run's pull request. The executor resolves all of that from the
344	task's `expected_outcome` before code-work starts and hands it in — code-work reads
345	`CLAUDINITE_TARGET_BRANCH` (the branch to push to), `CLAUDINITE_TARGET_PR` (the pull
346	request to push onto, set only when the run amends one) and `CLAUDINITE_TARGET_MODE`;
347	an agent session reads the same as `Target-branch:`, `Target-pr:` and `Supersedes:`
348	fields on its item. A code-work lane that lands a pull request takes them as
349	parameters (`deliverGenerated`'s `branch`/`pr`); a task with a pull request to report
350	names it in the hand-off payload's `delivered.pr`, which is what tells the executor a
351	`supersede_existing_pr` run's successor now exists.
352	
353	## The precondition is the ONLY decision point
354	
355	Task execution is **two similar, consecutive phases**: deterministic **code-work**
356	(a subprocess the executor runs, Action-side) and **agentic work** (the session
357	the executor hands off to, following task.md). Neither phase is "preparation" for the
358	other, and — the rule that matters — **neither may decide whether the task
359	runs**. That decision is the preconditions' alone:
360	
361	- A task whose preconditions hold **runs**. The later phases must not find
362	  "new reasons to skip" — not timing, not repo state, not "already handled", not
363	  an open PR elsewhere. If a condition should stop the run, it belongs in
364	  `preconditions`, as a named condition over signals.
365	- **Failures may stop a run** — a crash, a timeout, an API error park the
366	  item at a `task:status:needs-human-*`. Discretion may not.
367	- **A failing worker may say why it failed.** The executor sees an exit code and
368	  nothing more, so it cannot tell a token missing a scope (a person's five-second
369	  fix) from an exception in the worker's own code (a bug). A worker that knows
370	  prints one line on either stream before exiting non-zero, and the park is routed
371	  by it:
372	
373	  ```
374	  claudinite-needs-human: action — FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN lacks Actions: write
375	  ```
376	
377	  The kind is `action`, `decision`, `approval` or `failure`; the last marker in the
378	  output wins, so a worker sweeping many targets may revise its verdict as it goes.
379	  No marker — and every worker written before this existed — parks at `failure`,
380	  which is the lane that means "someone reads the trace".
381	- **"The work ran and produced nothing" is always legal** — that is an empty
382	  outcome, not a skip. The line: did the phase *do* the work and find it empty,
383	  or *decline* to do it?
384	- The conditional agent hand-off (a code-work worker requesting the agentic phase
385	  via `CLAUDINITE_REQUEST_AGENT`) escalates on **work code-work could not do** —
386	  never on a re-check of whether the run should have happened.
387	
388	The `task-phase-discipline` world check (advisory, heuristic) hunts for tasks
389	that escape this — skip-language in task.md, cycle-skip strings in code-work
390	workers.
391	
392	## Ordering between tasks is `schedule_after`, not a claim on the run
393	
394	A task that reads what another task produces declares **`schedule_after:
395	['<pack>/<task>']`**: its item yields while that upstream's item is live this
396	cycle, and picks up the moment the upstream converges. Nothing else
397	orders tasks — there is no run to claim, because there is no run: each item is
398	picked, decided and executed on its own, so a task that must go second says which
399	task it goes after and the queue holds it there.
400	
401	Declare it only for a real read-what-it-produces dependency, never as a general
402	priority hint, and never describe it as a `Blocked-by` edge — that is a different
403	field with different semantics. A yielded item is not spent: it waits, and runs in
404	the same cycle once the upstream is out of the way.
405	
406	## The queue labels are the item's state, and only the queue writes them
407	
408	A work item's **state is its labels**, and there is exactly one state label on it
409	at a time: `task:status:blocked` (waiting on a `Not-before` or a `Blocked-by`),
410	`task:status:waiting-for-executor` (available to pick), `task:status:running-executor`
411	(an executor holds the claim), `task:status:running-agent` (a session owns it).
412	Beside them: the item's lifelong `task:origin:*`, `task:urgent` (pick before anything
413	non-urgent), and the ends — `task:status:done`, `task:status:rejected`, and the four
414	`task:status:needs-human-*` parks. Every spelling any older engine wrote is still
415	read; none is written.
416	(A closed item may still wear the retired `outcome:*` spellings of the first two,
417	or `outcome:delivered`, which nothing writes any more; every reader accepts them.)
418	
419	Whether an item is a task's **standing occurrence** or an **ad-hoc run** is not a
420	label but a property of the item: the standing one is titled with the task and
421	nothing else, and its task is on a calendar. A `manual` task's item and every
422	qualified one — a fan-out target, a request naming its issue — are ad-hoc, which
423	is what lets them run beside the schedule rather than consuming it.
424	
425	Two rules follow, and both are about not borrowing the vocabulary:
426	
427	- **Never put a queue label on an ordinary issue**, from a task or by hand. The
428	  scheduler run and the executor read them as state, and a label on an issue that is not a
429	  `[claudinite-work]` item is either ignored or misread — neither is what the
430	  person applying it meant.
431	- **A task that wants its own tracking issue owns that issue's whole lifecycle**,
432	  in its own vocabulary. A park is the one state shared with the queue, and
433	  a task reusing it is on the hook for clearing it: nothing sweeps an issue that
434	  is not a work item.
435	
436	Label writes are always **granular** — add and remove named labels, never write
437	the label set. A set-write replaces from a stale snapshot and clobbers a
438	concurrent transition, and with a scheduler run and several executors moving labels at
439	once that is a correctness rule rather than a style preference.
440	
441	## An item's identity is its issue number, and a hand-off carries a nonce
442	
443	There is no slot id and no occurrence id beside the issue: **`#<n>` is the
444	occurrence**. It is what a `claudinite-task-exec` record's bracketed field
445	carries, and the only thing tying that record back to the work it describes.
446	
447	A hand-off is an **API call**, not a label event — the executor invokes the
448	session directly and stamps a nonce on the item first. So a session proves it is
449	this item's session in code before acting: the task file exists at HEAD, its pack
450	is declared, the title names that task, the item carries `task:status:running-agent`, and the
451	newest hand-off comment carries the nonce it was given. A nonce mismatch means
452	the fire named a hand-off that is not the current one — the item belongs to
453	someone else, or to an earlier episode — and the session stops without labelling,
454	closing or running anything.
455	
456	## Item lifecycle — every exit is terminal, and nothing keeps updating
457	
458	- **Succeeded, nothing pending** → `task:status:done`, one comment, issue closed.
459	- **Parked for a human** → one `task:status:needs-human-*` label naming what is being
460	  asked for, one comment, issue left open. Nothing keeps updating a parked issue:
461	  one visible convergence, then it is a person's to look at. Re-queueing it by hand
462	  (`create-work-item --wake #<n>`) is the sanctioned road back, and the
463	  precondition is re-evaluated at that pickup — which is what makes the retry safe
464	  even when the failed run half-did its work. The four:
465	  - `task:status:needs-human-approval` — succeeded, and deliberately left an unmerged PR
466	    for a person to merge or close. The only park that is not a fault. `--pr` names that
467	    PR, and any park may name what would end it: the item then closes by itself when
468	    the target resolves, `done` if it merged and `rejected` if it did not.
469	  - `task:status:needs-human-action` — something outside the code must change before this
470	    can run: a secret set, a scope granted, a routine rewired, an input supplied.
471	  - `task:status:needs-human-decision` — the run stopped mid-flight and the next step is a
472	    choice: re-queue or abandon, does the half-done work stand, was the ceiling
473	    violation acceptable.
474	  - `task:status:needs-human-failure` — the run broke. A bug, a contract-forbidden shape, a
475	    malformed item. The default when nothing else fits.
476	
477	  **An open item is the task's standing item, and a `failure` park therefore stops
478	  the task being scheduled** — no further occurrence is filed until it is woken or
479	  closed. That is deliberate: a queue of items that will break the same way helps
480	  nobody, and the silence is the signal. The other three do **not** hold the lane —
481	  they are one person's inbox, not a fault in the task, so the schedule carries on
482	  around them.
483	- **Never ran** → `task:status:rejected`, closed as not planned: the precondition
484	  declined, or the task is gone (file removed, pack undeclared). An obsolete item
485	  is not an anomaly and gets no park. A scheduled task's next occurrence
486	  is the scheduler run's ask at its next anchor — and most declines never make an
487	  item at all: the scheduler run asks the precondition when the anchor comes,
488	  files an item only on a yes, and records a no as a row on the repo's schedule
489	  board.
490	- Every terminal state is recorded in code as a `claudinite-task-exec` line
491	  (`record-exec.mjs`), so the usage fold counts task statuses out of the captured
492	  conversation logs deterministically.
493	
494	## A dormant project runs nothing
495	
496	A project nobody is working on declares itself dormant in `.claudinite-settings.json`:
497	
498	```json
499	"dormant": true
500	```
501	
502	The scheduler run instantiates, readies and reclaims nothing, and the executor picks
503	nothing up; the fleet sweeps skip it; sessions are unaffected. Delete it to wake — a dormant spell is not replayed, so the repo
504	simply starts scheduling again from now.
505

# claudinite-tasks — scheduled work

Everything whose subject is task work: the work-item queue, the executor, the task contract and
its signals, calendar/anchor math, run records, code-work, and the delivery lane a task's output
lands through. Declaring this pack is what gives a repo scheduled work; a repo that does not
declare it runs none, which is a supported state rather than a degraded one.

The mechanism itself — the state machine, the generator, the executor's protocol, urgency and
forcing, recovery — is the canon's own tasks-dispatch design document, and authoring a task is the
`writing-tasks` skill's subject. This file is the pack's own map.

## Layout

| Path | What lives there |
|---|---|

## `shared-code/` — the one sanctioned cross-pack import

Another pack's code may import `packs/claudinite-tasks/shared-code/*`, and nothing else of this
pack. The `pack-independence` barrier's allow list names that directory; no other pack gains an
equivalent surface by existing.

| Module | What it publishes | Who reads it |
|---|---|---|
| `work-items.mjs` | the title grammar that is a work item's identity, the outcome/status decode over its labels, lease state, the dispatch vocabulary, and what a scheduler run would instantiate | claudinite-dashboard, claudinite-fleet-sheepdog |
| `anchors.mjs` | period length, and the instant a task's window last opened at or opens next | claudinite-dashboard |
| `delivery.mjs` | `landPr`, `deliverGenerated` — how a task's output becomes a landed PR or a regenerated file | any pack whose tasks deliver |
| `github.mjs` | the GitHub client and REST helpers, and the tracker issue a worker records on | any pack whose tasks reach GitHub |
| `signals.mjs` | the signal shapes a precondition is handed | packs asserting what their own tasks will see |
| `task-contract.mjs` | task-declaration validation, and the signal union either precondition form resolves to | every pack with tasks, in its own tests |
| `preconditions.mjs` | the precondition vocabulary, the expression grammar, and the one seam that turns a task plus its signals into a verdict — the call the executor makes at pick | every pack with tasks, in its own tests |
| `merge-policy.mjs` | the auto-merge policy verdict (`automerge`, the `Merge:` field, the arming trailer) and the `merge-rules.json` compiler | any pack declaring policies or merge rules, in its own tests |
| `usage-format.mjs` | the usage aggregate's codec | claudinite-fleet-sheepdog's fleet-wide aggregator |

A pack whose **non-task** code reads any of these declares `requires: ['claudinite-tasks']`. A
pack's `tasks/` folder needs no declaration: a mount without this pack carries no `tasks/` at all,
since a task folder is inert without the queue that runs it.

## Adoption

The two workflow files and the routine endpoints cannot converge into place — `.github/workflows/`
is the one directory a member's nightly update may never write — so they are scaffolded once, at
adoption, by the `adopt-pack` skill. They are static from then on: the per-repo cron minute and
anchor hours are written once, secrets travel as one fixed line, and the `run:` lines name mount
pack paths behind which everything converges nightly.

## The legacy `engine/scheduler/` shims

Until #1317's execution chain finishes, `engine/scheduler/*` still exists as one-line re-exports of
this pack, for members whose vendored workers, workflow `run:` lines and stored routine prompts
still name the old paths. They ship only into a mount that carries this pack, and they are deleted
once no fielded member names one.

## Checks

| Rule | Confidence | Dimension | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| `task-declaration-shape` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
| `task-code-work-env` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
| `automerge-policy-scope` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
| `legacy-task-fields` | low | complexity | check: advisory |

The first two are relevance-first — inert until the repo carries a `tasks/<name>/task.json` of its own; the third is self-gating on the branch's own arming trailer.

- `task-declaration-shape` — a task declaration the scheduler reads is incomplete or illegal — no `preconditions` saying when it runs, an unknown condition, an illegal value — so the task never fires or fires wrong.
- `task-code-work-env` — a task reads a `CLAUDINITE_*` variable code-work never sets, so a parameter (a scope filter, a dry-run switch) silently never arrives and the run goes green in its most dangerous mode.
- `automerge-policy-scope` — a branch that stamped the `Claudinite-Automerge-Policy` trailer (its run intends to land its own PR) carries a diff its declared policy does not cover, which is exactly the unreviewed change the policy exists to stop.

content.content:
One row per scheduled task, one cell per day column, at the day's anchor. A cell's state is
carried by **form and the semantic set**, so it reads in either theme:

| State | Cell | Read from |
|---|---|---|
| **ran** | filled, good | a closed item of that task with `outcome:done` / `delivered`, by `closed_at` |
| **asked, declined** | hollow, muted | a closed item with `outcome:obsolete`, or the schedule board's `verdict: no` for that ask |
| **parked** | filled, amber | an open item of that task at `needs-human-approval` (it waits for a person) |
| **failure park** | hatched, critical stroke | an open item at `needs-human-failure`, placed on the day it parked; `◂` at the left edge when older than the window |
| **predicted** | hollow, the machine's blue | the next anchor for a task whose last verdict on the board was `go` or `fail-open` |
| **will decline** | **half-height** hollow, muted | the next anchor for a task whose last verdict was `no` |
| **running** | filled circle at *now* | `task:status:running-agent` |

A day with more than one occurrence carries the count *in* the cell in mono (`4`, `7`); the
hover names the tasks and their outcomes. Predicted and declined are told apart by height,
never by dash pattern, which at 3 px is invisible.

**A failure park lands on its own task's row**, followed by whatever the task did after it.
The roster reads such a park as *the lane is held — nothing new is scheduled*; a hatched cell
followed by filled cells is the record disagreeing, read left to right on one line. There is
no separate "held lanes" row, because the contradiction is a row fact.

## Tomorrow's human workload

The Now group's header sentence, derived, never a tile: **the PRs waiting now, plus the
scheduled runs whose declaration cannot land their own PR** — `automerge: 'nothing'` — plus
the runs whose policy covers only local packs and habitually write wider (currently parked on
approval). Each predicted cell of such a task carries `+1` in the lane and the row ends in
`+1 PR / day`; the sentence reads `21 open PRs · every one waits for a person · +1 a day from
growth-promote, 2–4 on Sunday`. It is the declarations' `automerge` field read against the
schedule board's `next window`, not a guess.

## The quiet tail

One ruled line under the board: `50 issues, quiet — plain, on no edge`, then three counts in
mono — **rotting** (`updated_at` ≥ 14 d), **quick-win**, **needs-decision** — and a `show ▾`
---
| **pending PR** | *waits for*: the policy expression and the run's own `AUTOMERGE:` sentence; *closes / ends*: the `Closes #n` or `Ends-when` target and what the queue does on merge against close; *unblocks*: reverse `Blocked-by` hits; *size · CI*: **not read** until the PR page and the head sha's checks are fetched; *left by*: the item, its model, session, claim → hand-off → converge timestamps | PR body, item body, item comments (`CLAIM_MARKER`, `HANDOFF_MARKER`, the converge comment) |
| **failed task** | *last run*: claim, nonce, session, what it delivered and the PR it left (merged?); *what broke*: the converge comment's own sentence; *park history*: which janitor rule parked it, when, whether it was re-queued or superseded, and the later runs of the same task with their outcomes; *lane*: what the roster claims against what the record shows; *do*: the `converge-item` command | item comments, closed items of the same task |
| **stuck ad-hoc item** | the chain as a list: each `Blocked-by` target with its state and *who is scheduled to move it* (a task, a PR, nobody); the janitor's stuck-dependency comment and its date; the age of the premise — `created_at` and the latest `main` commit touching the paths it names; its `Automerge:` policy as the landing it will get; *do*: close the blocker, mark it ad-hoc, or re-scope | body lines, blocker issues, janitor comment |
| **plain issue** | age and idle; *blocks*: reverse edges and, transitively, the rows it holds; *who moves it*: no mark, no `Task:` field, no PR `Closes` it; *rot*: idle against the 14 d bar and whether its premise moved (a later issue or merge naming the same subject); *quick-win*: the label, and what closing it unblocks; *do* | labels, reverse edges, PR bodies |
| **scheduled task** | the last N occurrences as a strip with outcome words and the decline reasons from the schedule board; next anchor; `agent_model`, `expected_outcome`, `automerge`; cost per run from the fold's `taskCost`; the PRs it has left open | task declaration, the schedule board, fold, PR listing |
| **park** | approval: as pending PR (it *is* the PR); action and decision: the converge comment's ask, verbatim, and the `Ends-when` / `Retry-every` that would close it without a person | item comments, body lines |

## Limits it reports rather than hides

- **Issue history is a window** — the most recent few hundred issues, not all of
  them. Outside it, a task's history reads as "none in window", never "never run".
  The footer states which.
- **Declaration fields are lifted as text**, because there is nothing to `import`
  when reading another repo over the API. A field it cannot read renders *unknown*
  and is never defaulted — a confident wrong cadence would move a next-anchor the
  roster is read for.
- **The past-data half is only as fresh as the repo's last fold**, which the footer
  states separately from this load's own time. A repo that folds nothing has no past
  half at all, and the panels that wanted it say which task writes the file.
- **Which tasks a given hour *evaluated* is not shown**, only what executed. Nothing in
  a run listing names a task, and reading each run's job log to find out would be two
  API calls per run — the cost the fold itself dropped for the same reason. Why a task
  declined its last ask is on its own row instead, from the verdict the item carries.

content.content:
closed issues keep theirs, and fielded engines keep writing their own spellings
until they converge. Every decoder maps every spelling ever written straight to
its canonical status, in one pass:

| legacy | canonical |
|---|---|
| `task:blocked`, `task:ready`, `task:executing`, `task:agent` | the four live statuses, in order |
| `needs-human` + `task:needs-human-<kind>` | `task:status:needs-human-<kind>` (the sub-label decides; bare or unknown → `failure`) |
| `task:done`, `outcome:done` | `task:status:done` |
| `task:obsolete`, `outcome:obsolete` | `task:status:rejected` |
| `outcome:delivered` | recognized forever as the historical "delivered" outcome — an unmerged PR parks at `needs-human-approval` now, and nothing writes it |
| `origin:schedule` | inert stored data (§3) |
| the `claude-*` request vocabulary | the one-issue request shapes (§16.1) |

The map never shrinks, and legacy label *definitions* are never deleted from a
repo — deleting a label strips it from closed issues too, which is stored data.
Two things bind the fielded surface: the executor workflow's event trigger
names label strings literally, so it accepts the legacy ready/urgent spellings
for as long as any fielded engine writes them; and the legacy constants stay
exported for the pack workers that import them.

**Only a `failure` park holds the task's lane** (§5). An open unqualified item
of a scheduled task *is* its standing item (§3), so while one exists no further
occurrence is filed — for a break that is the point, since a queue of items that will fail the
same way helps nobody and the silence is the signal. For the other three it is a
bug: a PR waiting on a reviewer, a decision waiting on its owner and a secret
waiting to be set are one person's inbox, not a fault in the task, and #1032
measured what conflating them costs — a permission gap parked `missingbulb/Shepherd`'s
`fleet-digest` for two days while its dashboard read healthy, because no item was
ever filed behind the parked one. So the generator drops non-blocking parks from
both the standing-item test and the duplicate sweep beside it.

This is the sketch's lifecycle with two adjustments, both argued for rather
than assumed:

- **Executor identity is a claim comment, not a label.** The sketch's
  `being-handled-by-executor-1` puts an unbounded set (executor identities) into
  a vocabulary that must stay small and queryable; every new executor would mint
  a label, and a query for "what is executing" would have to know every
  executor's name. One state label (`task:status:running-executor`) answers the query; the
  claim comment — which the lease protocol requires anyway — carries *who*
  (executor id, run URL) and *when*. Same for `task:status:running-agent`: the hand-off
  comment names the CCR session.
- **`succeeded-with-unexpected-result` became `outcome:delivered`, and then
  became a park.** "Unexpected" would blur two things that must not blur: a run
  that legitimately left a pending artifact within its ceiling (a `pr` task whose
  automerge is `nothing` → open PR: *expected*, but the world hasn't finished with it), and a run that
  violated its ceiling (a `none` task that opened a PR). The second is still a
  **failure**, now `task:status:needs-human-decision` — someone must say whether the
  overreach stands — exactly as `verify-outcome` enforces. The first turned out
  not to be a terminal state at all: a PR nobody has merged is waiting on a
  named person, and closing the item hid that from every surface that counts
  open work, so it parks at `task:status:needs-human-approval` and stays open. It does
  not hold the lane, so the reviewer's silence delays only the review.

Terminal-state discipline is unchanged: every item converges exactly once to
exactly one end — one of the two terminal statuses, or a park under one of the
four kinds — with one comment saying what happened.

**Label writes are granular, always** ([RESEARCH](RESEARCH.md) §2): add and
remove named labels (REST POST/DELETE), never write the label *set* (PUT,
GraphQL `updateIssue`) — a set-write replaces from a stale snapshot and
clobbers concurrent transitions, a bug class GitHub's own CLI shipped
([cli/cli#4861](https://github.com/cli/cli/pull/4861)). With multiple
executors and a scheduler run all moving labels, this is a correctness rule, not a
style preference.

**The road back from a park** (SCENARIOS S12/S19, F7): a human who has
resolved the cause re-queues the item by removing the park status and applying
`task:status:waiting-for-executor` — the sanctioned retry lever, write-gated
like every label operation here. The next pickup re-runs the precondition
(§6.4), which is what makes the retry safe even when the failed run half-did
its work. Alternatively the human closes the item (optionally superseding it
with a forced retry, §8); nothing mechanical ever re-queues a parked item.

## 5. The generator — decide at the anchor, file only work

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/writing-tests

# Testing practices

A consuming repo's own test *mechanics* — runner, layout, which suites exist — are its own docs'; CI-trigger rules and the `GITHUB_TOKEN` workflow-recursion gotcha are [git-github-advanced](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md)'s.

- See a test fail before you trust it: write it red before the fix (green after), or break what it guards and watch it go red. A test that has never failed proves nothing. For a **refusal/negative** test — one asserting a guard yields *nothing* — the write-it-red-first branch is unavailable: the pre-change code also yielded nothing, so the test passes from birth and proves nothing. See-it-fail there **must** be the second method — mutate the new guard (weaken it), watch the test bite, then restore it. Restore with `git checkout -- <file>` (or `git stash`) taken at the moment of mutating — never a `.bak` copy saved earlier, which predates whatever else you edited in between and silently discards that intervening work.
- A mechanism meant to survive a retry, re-queue, or hand-off needs a test that calls it twice, not once. A suite of single-call tests stays green while the multi-call case corrupts state — the double-call is what a real retry, requeue, or hand-off actually does. When the mechanism arbitrates by identity (a claim, a lock), the second call must come from a **different actor**: a single actor retrying its own stale claim can't expose an identity-masked race, since it still recognizes its own claim as valid.
- A simulator of a stateful mechanism must advance state only where the real engine's code actually leaves a mark — never wherever the rule's stated description says a transition happens. A sim that fires on every event matching the rule's *intent* is correct by construction against that rule and blind to exactly the silent paths where the real implementation and the rule have quietly diverged — which is where a genuine bug usually lives. Read the real engine's code for what it *writes*, and model that.
- Before trusting a new transform/normalizer, run it over the *real existing corpus* it will process, not just hand-picked test inputs — the live data exposes edge cases your examples won't. Relatedly, prefer a generic structural rule over a hand-maintained list of special cases: the enumerated list needs per-instance upkeep and silently has gaps, while a rule keyed on structure (e.g. "a known registry label under any 2-letter ccTLD") covers the whole class at once. (3)
- A test that stubs the exact boundary where the bug lives can't catch that bug — it guards only the shape it asserts, not the runtime effect. Say what it can't catch.
- A test that dereferences a path inside a **read-only dependency tree someone else refreshes** — a vendored mount, a synced submodule, generated output from an upstream build — is a test whose fixture a stranger can delete: the day upstream retires that file the case fails `ENOENT` with nothing in your repo having changed. Assert against a path only when the test itself creates it; when a case genuinely needs an upstream file, read it **defensively** and skip with a stated reason if it is gone, so a retirement upstream reports as "no longer applicable" rather than as your repo being broken. Check what actually runs these cases too — a suite that the repo's own gate never invokes reports its breakage to whoever happens to look.
- **Never pin a declaration to itself.** Asserting that a config/manifest field equals the literal it is declared with (`assert.equal(task.expected_outcome, 'pr')`, `assert.equal(pack.id, 'thing')`) restates the file under test in a second file. It can only fail when someone changes the value **on purpose**, so it catches no defect and instead taxes every deliberate change with a mirrored edit — and, worse, teaches that the value is load-bearing prose to be restated, which is how one setting ends up copied into a comment, a worker doc, a README table and a test, so flipping it becomes a five-file diff. The see-it-fail test exposes it: to make the assertion go red you must break the thing it asserts, which is not a bug. Assert what can actually come apart — a claim spanning two artifacts that could drift independently: the doc a field *names* exists; every signal the code reads is declared; two implementations of the same list agree; a value the runtime constrains is inside its legal set. If a declaration genuinely must not change without deliberation, that is a review concern, not a test.
- Prefer a single shared double; but when a subsystem is faked by more than one (a minimal unit stub vs. a faithful harness that boots the real module), a new call into the faked surface must be taught to **every** double, or the untaught one breaks — and the faithful harness turns an unmodeled API into a confusing **far-away** failure (a DOM-snapshot pixel-diff, not a local error at the call site). After adding a call into a faked boundary, find every double of it and extend each.
- When one wire format, encoding, or algorithm is **implemented twice** — two languages, two tiers, a hand-rolled client encoder against the server's library — no compiler, type system, or single test run spans the two, so the only thing holding them together is a **shared vector set carried deliberately by both suites**: the same inputs and the same expected outputs, asserted independently on each side, including the boundary cases the two could plausibly round differently (a value exactly on a bisection midpoint, a tie, a truncation edge). A vector asserted on only one side is an input nobody ever compared — both suites stay green, in different languages under different runners, while the claim quietly stops covering it. So: touching *either* implementation re-runs *both* suites, and adding a vector adds it to both. Where the pairing is mechanical (the two vector lists must contain the same inputs), pin it with a check rather than a convention.
- A traceability/coverage gate that requires every spec item be *claimed* by some test of one fixed kind proves only that it's claimed, not that it's verified. When items differ in kind, the gate green-lights claims that kind can't check — a pixel snapshot "covers" a click's tab-opening it can never observe, or a state the case never renders (and can't, when the data can't reach it). Segment the gate by the verification each item needs (route behavior to a behavior test, rendering to a snapshot) rather than forcing every item onto one mechanism. (1)
- A golden/snapshot test whose expected artifact is hand-authored to mirror what production renders is a parallel implementation: it drifts from the real output and can't catch changes to the renderer (a hand-built UI gallery even faked a state the app never shows). Drive the snapshot through the real code path, faking only its inputs.
- A snapshot/golden test that depends on the current date/time must inject a fixed reference instant, not read the real clock — else a fixed-date fixture silently rots as wall-clock time passes ("this year" becomes "past" next year). Thread the reference time through the code under test, defaulting to the real clock in production. When retrofitting such a rule into an existing fixture suite, pin the reference instant so existing fixtures land on the same side they were authored for — so only the cases that deliberately exercise the new rule change and the diff stays small and reviewable, rather than a sprawling baseline churn that buries the intended change.
- A round-trip test that asserts by comparing **serialized** forms (`JSON.stringify(decoded) === JSON.stringify(original)`) silently makes key *order* part of the contract: add a field at the top of the encoder's record and append it in the decoder's, and the round-trip fails on ordering alone — with a diff that reads like a data bug and sends you after a value that was correct all along. Deep-equal the parsed structures instead, so the test states what it means; keep serialized comparison only where byte-identity is genuinely the property under test, and say so in the test.
- A new **e2e / heavy-browser** test must go green at least twice in CI before merging — one green run doesn't rule out a flake. This applies only to that class (the real-Chrome `test/fullBrowserHeavyTests/` suites); the deterministic offline/unit/integration tests don't touch a live browser or network, so one green run is enough for them.
- A test that can only run remotely (e.g. CI-only) must diagnose itself: on failure, dump the observed state, not just an assertion. It must also be *hang-proof* — bound every `await` (a timeout race) and set a test-level timeout — so a failure fails fast with that diagnostic instead of burning the whole job's timeout. An unbounded await on something that never settles (e.g. a callback that silently never fires) turns a 5-second failure into a 20-minute hang, and each CI-only iteration already costs a full round-trip.
- Run a suite you know is slow as **its own command with an explicit timeout well above its measured runtime**, and do the dependency install as a *separate, earlier* call. An agent shell caps a command at a default (order of a couple of minutes) and pushes it to the background when it expires; the reflex is then to start the suite over, so one green result costs double the wall clock with two suites racing each other. Chaining setup in front of the suite is what usually pushes the pair past the cap. If a run does get backgrounded, wait on the one already running rather than launching a second.
- To test code that drives a real browser or other external runtime in CI, prefer a *self-authored hermetic input* (e.g. a `data:` URL whose own script reproduces the behavior) over hitting a live third-party target — the live target is non-deterministic and often bot-blocked from a CI/datacenter IP, so it flakes or can't run, while a self-authored input exercises the same engine deterministically. (2)
- Gate a fuzzy quality metric (a coverage %, not a binary pass) behind a high-watermark: refresh the artifact and ratchet the watermark up locally, keep CI read-only (assert against the committed baseline, never rewrite it), and re-baseline by hand only when a deliberate change legitimately moves it — a number that can only climb catches a silent regression without flapping on noise. When the population it covers can *grow* (e.g. new test cases), store the set the watermark was computed over and gate only over the cases shared with it, so a newly added item is excluded rather than dragging the aggregate below the bar; re-anchor the watermark when the set changes. (A single aggregate watermark can then be re-anchored over a regression bundled into the *same* change as a set change — store per-item bars if that must be caught.)
- For behavior a person must sign off on (a third-party integration, an extraction result), keep a layer of declarative, human-reviewed expectation files — distinct from the unit tests, which nobody reads for *intent* — and cover every behavior change with a minimal, representative case there (one behavior per case, no incidental complexity), since that case is what gets reviewed.
- When a snapshot/golden test fails because the output *legitimately* moved (the pixels or bytes changed for a real reason), don't quietly regenerate the baseline to go green — an unreviewed baseline change is an unreviewed behavior change. Surface the diff (committed **expected**, newly-rendered **actual**, highlighted **diff**) and get owner approval before re-baselining; until then keep the *reverted* baseline committed so the branch honestly shows the test red-pending — never commit the new baseline first.
- When a test asserts exact values extracted from a captured artifact (a cached page, a recorded response), record and commit the artifact *first*, then read the expected values off the committed file — don't hand-write the expectations from memory or a live view and hope they match. Guessing the value desyncs the test from the real fixture; reading it off the committed bytes can't.
- A test that maintains a committed artifact should regenerate it into the working tree deterministically (no timestamps, so an unchanged run yields no diff) and skip the write under CI — never shell out to git from a test. Commit the artifact through the normal review flow, like a snapshot.
- Render a UI *image* golden with the engine that matches the surface, and prefer the deterministic one. A surface that is inline-styled SVG, or flexbox-only markup authored for it, renders **bit-exact** through a headless rasterizer (e.g. satori → SVG, resvg → PNG) driven by the shipped code, using **bundled** fonts, never system fonts, and a pinned locale — demand a **zero-pixel** diff there. But that rasterizer has no CSS engine and draws no native widgets: a full shipped page using CSS **grid**, custom properties (`var()`), `@media`, **emoji**, or **form controls** (a range slider, radio, `<select>`) is beyond it — screenshot that with a **headless browser** instead, and allow a *small* diff tolerance (browser antialiasing varies across machines, so it isn't bit-exact). Match the engine to the surface; never reshape the product to fit the rasterizer. (A rasterized popup golden works only because the popup was authored flexbox-only — the moment a surface needs grid/vars/widgets, it needs a browser.) Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/writing-tests

# Testing practices

A consuming repo's own test *mechanics* — runner, layout, which suites exist — are its own docs'; CI-trigger rules and the `GITHUB_TOKEN` workflow-recursion gotcha are [git-github-advanced](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md)'s.

- See a test fail before you trust it: write it red before the fix (green after), or break what it guards and watch it go red. A test that has never failed proves nothing. For a **refusal/negative** test — one asserting a guard yields *nothing* — the write-it-red-first branch is unavailable: the pre-change code also yielded nothing, so the test passes from birth and proves nothing. See-it-fail there **must** be the second method — mutate the new guard (weaken it), watch the test bite, then restore it. Restore with `git checkout -- <file>` (or `git stash`) taken at the moment of mutating — never a `.bak` copy saved earlier, which predates whatever else you edited in between and silently discards that intervening work.
- A mechanism meant to survive a retry, re-queue, or hand-off needs a test that calls it twice, not once. A suite of single-call tests stays green while the multi-call case corrupts state — the double-call is what a real retry, requeue, or hand-off actually does. When the mechanism arbitrates by identity (a claim, a lock), the second call must come from a **different actor**: a single actor retrying its own stale claim can't expose an identity-masked race, since it still recognizes its own claim as valid.
- A simulator of a stateful mechanism must advance state only where the real engine's code actually leaves a mark — never wherever the rule's stated description says a transition happens. A sim that fires on every event matching the rule's *intent* is correct by construction against that rule and blind to exactly the silent paths where the real implementation and the rule have quietly diverged — which is where a genuine bug usually lives. Read the real engine's code for what it *writes*, and model that.
- Before trusting a new transform/normalizer, run it over the *real existing corpus* it will process, not just hand-picked test inputs — the live data exposes edge cases your examples won't. Relatedly, prefer a generic structural rule over a hand-maintained list of special cases: the enumerated list needs per-instance upkeep and silently has gaps, while a rule keyed on structure (e.g. "a known registry label under any 2-letter ccTLD") covers the whole class at once. (3)
- A test that stubs the exact boundary where the bug lives can't catch that bug — it guards only the shape it asserts, not the runtime effect. Say what it can't catch.
- A test that dereferences a path inside a **read-only dependency tree someone else refreshes** — a vendored mount, a synced submodule, generated output from an upstream build — is a test whose fixture a stranger can delete: the day upstream retires that file the case fails `ENOENT` with nothing in your repo having changed. Assert against a path only when the test itself creates it; when a case genuinely needs an upstream file, read it **defensively** and skip with a stated reason if it is gone, so a retirement upstream reports as "no longer applicable" rather than as your repo being broken. Check what actually runs these cases too — a suite that the repo's own gate never invokes reports its breakage to whoever happens to look.
- **Never pin a declaration to itself.** Asserting that a config/manifest field equals the literal it is declared with (`assert.equal(task.expected_outcome, 'pr')`, `assert.equal(pack.id, 'thing')`) restates the file under test in a second file. It can only fail when someone changes the value **on purpose**, so it catches no defect and instead taxes every deliberate change with a mirrored edit — and, worse, teaches that the value is load-bearing prose to be restated, which is how one setting ends up copied into a comment, a worker doc, a README table and a test, so flipping it becomes a five-file diff. The see-it-fail test exposes it: to make the assertion go red you must break the thing it asserts, which is not a bug. Assert what can actually come apart — a claim spanning two artifacts that could drift independently: the doc a field *names* exists; every signal the code reads is declared; two implementations of the same list agree; a value the runtime constrains is inside its legal set. If a declaration genuinely must not change without deliberation, that is a review concern, not a test.
- Prefer a single shared double; but when a subsystem is faked by more than one (a minimal unit stub vs. a faithful harness that boots the real module), a new call into the faked surface must be taught to **every** double, or the untaught one breaks — and the faithful harness turns an unmodeled API into a confusing **far-away** failure (a DOM-snapshot pixel-diff, not a local error at the call site). After adding a call into a faked boundary, find every double of it and extend each.
- When one wire format, encoding, or algorithm is **implemented twice** — two languages, two tiers, a hand-rolled client encoder against the server's library — no compiler, type system, or single test run spans the two, so the only thing holding them together is a **shared vector set carried deliberately by both suites**: the same inputs and the same expected outputs, asserted independently on each side, including the boundary cases the two could plausibly round differently (a value exactly on a bisection midpoint, a tie, a truncation edge). A vector asserted on only one side is an input nobody ever compared — both suites stay green, in different languages under different runners, while the claim quietly stops covering it. So: touching *either* implementation re-runs *both* suites, and adding a vector adds it to both. Where the pairing is mechanical (the two vector lists must contain the same inputs), pin it with a check rather than a convention.
- A traceability/coverage gate that requires every spec item be *claimed* by some test of one fixed kind proves only that it's claimed, not that it's verified. When items differ in kind, the gate green-lights claims that kind can't check — a pixel snapshot "covers" a click's tab-opening it can never observe, or a state the case never renders (and can't, when the data can't reach it). Segment the gate by the verification each item needs (route behavior to a behavior test, rendering to a snapshot) rather than forcing every item onto one mechanism. (1)
- A golden/snapshot test whose expected artifact is hand-authored to mirror what production renders is a parallel implementation: it drifts from the real output and can't catch changes to the renderer (a hand-built UI gallery even faked a state the app never shows). Drive the snapshot through the real code path, faking only its inputs.
- A snapshot/golden test that depends on the current date/time must inject a fixed reference instant, not read the real clock — else a fixed-date fixture silently rots as wall-clock time passes ("this year" becomes "past" next year). Thread the reference time through the code under test, defaulting to the real clock in production. When retrofitting such a rule into an existing fixture suite, pin the reference instant so existing fixtures land on the same side they were authored for — so only the cases that deliberately exercise the new rule change and the diff stays small and reviewable, rather than a sprawling baseline churn that buries the intended change.
- A round-trip test that asserts by comparing **serialized** forms (`JSON.stringify(decoded) === JSON.stringify(original)`) silently makes key *order* part of the contract: add a field at the top of the encoder's record and append it in the decoder's, and the round-trip fails on ordering alone — with a diff that reads like a data bug and sends you after a value that was correct all along. Deep-equal the parsed structures instead, so the test states what it means; keep serialized comparison only where byte-identity is genuinely the property under test, and say so in the test.
- A new **e2e / heavy-browser** test must go green at least twice in CI before merging — one green run doesn't rule out a flake. This applies only to that class (the real-Chrome `test/fullBrowserHeavyTests/` suites); the deterministic offline/unit/integration tests don't touch a live browser or network, so one green run is enough for them.
- A test that can only run remotely (e.g. CI-only) must diagnose itself: on failure, dump the observed state, not just an assertion. It must also be *hang-proof* — bound every `await` (a timeout race) and set a test-level timeout — so a failure fails fast with that diagnostic instead of burning the whole job's timeout. An unbounded await on something that never settles (e.g. a callback that silently never fires) turns a 5-second failure into a 20-minute hang, and each CI-only iteration already costs a full round-trip.
- Run a suite you know is slow as **its own command with an explicit timeout well above its measured runtime**, and do the dependency install as a *separate, earlier* call. An agent shell caps a command at a default (order of a couple of minutes) and pushes it to the background when it expires; the reflex is then to start the suite over, so one green result costs double the wall clock with two suites racing each other. Chaining setup in front of the suite is what usually pushes the pair past the cap. If a run does get backgrounded, wait on the one already running rather than launching a second.
- To test code that drives a real browser or other external runtime in CI, prefer a *self-authored hermetic input* (e.g. a `data:` URL whose own script reproduces the behavior) over hitting a live third-party target — the live target is non-deterministic and often bot-blocked from a CI/datacenter IP, so it flakes or can't run, while a self-authored input exercises the same engine deterministically. (2)
- Gate a fuzzy quality metric (a coverage %, not a binary pass) behind a high-watermark: refresh the artifact and ratchet the watermark up locally, keep CI read-only (assert against the committed baseline, never rewrite it), and re-baseline by hand only when a deliberate change legitimately moves it — a number that can only climb catches a silent regression without flapping on noise. When the population it covers can *grow* (e.g. new test cases), store the set the watermark was computed over and gate only over the cases shared with it, so a newly added item is excluded rather than dragging the aggregate below the bar; re-anchor the watermark when the set changes. (A single aggregate watermark can then be re-anchored over a regression bundled into the *same* change as a set change — store per-item bars if that must be caught.)
- For behavior a person must sign off on (a third-party integration, an extraction result), keep a layer of declarative, human-reviewed expectation files — distinct from the unit tests, which nobody reads for *intent* — and cover every behavior change with a minimal, representative case there (one behavior per case, no incidental complexity), since that case is what gets reviewed.
- When a snapshot/golden test fails because the output *legitimately* moved (the pixels or bytes changed for a real reason), don't quietly regenerate the baseline to go green — an unreviewed baseline change is an unreviewed behavior change. Surface the diff (committed **expected**, newly-rendered **actual**, highlighted **diff**) and get owner approval before re-baselining; until then keep the *reverted* baseline committed so the branch honestly shows the test red-pending — never commit the new baseline first.
- When a test asserts exact values extracted from a captured artifact (a cached page, a recorded response), record and commit the artifact *first*, then read the expected values off the committed file — don't hand-write the expectations from memory or a live view and hope they match. Guessing the value desyncs the test from the real fixture; reading it off the committed bytes can't.
- A test that maintains a committed artifact should regenerate it into the working tree deterministically (no timestamps, so an unchanged run yields no diff) and skip the write under CI — never shell out to git from a test. Commit the artifact through the normal review flow, like a snapshot.
- Render a UI *image* golden with the engine that matches the surface, and prefer the deterministic one. A surface that is inline-styled SVG, or flexbox-only markup authored for it, renders **bit-exact** through a headless rasterizer (e.g. satori → SVG, resvg → PNG) driven by the shipped code, using **bundled** fonts, never system fonts, and a pinned locale — demand a **zero-pixel** diff there. But that rasterizer has no CSS engine and draws no native widgets: a full shipped page using CSS **grid**, custom properties (`var()`), `@media`, **emoji**, or **form controls** (a range slider, radio, `<select>`) is beyond it — screenshot that with a **headless browser** instead, and allow a *small* diff tolerance (browser antialiasing varies across machines, so it isn't bit-exact). Match the engine to the surface; never reshape the product to fit the rasterizer. (A rasterized popup golden works only because the popup was authored flexbox-only — the moment a surface needs grid/vars/widgets, it needs a browser.) Since the browser goldens aren't gate-able bit-exact and a runner may lack the browser, let those cases **self-skip** where it's absent so the deterministic cases still gate.
- To image-golden a surface your code **injects into a host page** (a control mounted into a third-party toolbar), render it against a **committed capture of the real host DOM with its computed styles flattened inline** — the deterministic rasterizer reads only inline styles, and the host's own stylesheet is not yours to ship. Mount it with the **shipped injector** (so the golden proves the placement, not a hand-placed copy), and name the model's boundary honestly: substituted icon-font glyphs, an approximated host chrome (a captured sample is spec, not folklore — the origin lesson of a supported-targets matrix).

1125	Actions bills each job's runtime rounded **up** to the next minute, so a
1126	day's cost is the workflow-run count, not the minutes worked — and the
1127	one-item run (§15.22) paid a whole invocation of checkout, setup and rounding
1128	per item, with the hourly drain dispatched even into an empty queue. The
1129	reversal (§15.30): a run drains until nothing is pickable, the drain job
1130	dispatches only when the scheduler run left something pickable, and the hold
1131	is re-read between items. The accounting (`actionExecutions()`) counts every
1132	billed run — a suspended start included, since the runner still spins up to
1133	read the hold — by workflow and, for the executor, by recorded trigger. S34,
1134	S36 and S37 above replay under the new run boundary; the two scenarios here
1135	pin the bill itself.
1136	
1137	### S65 — a working day's bill
1138	
1139	A full day of scheduled work — the 02:00/03:00/04:00 morning chain, tidy,
1140	a release — plus ad-hoc work: a marked request and a hand-created item of a
1141	manual task. Seven pieces of work converge for exactly **29 invocations**:
1142	the cron's 24 scheduler runs (the floor), one drain per hour that had work
