A change under packs/<id>/ no longer bumps that pack's version itself. The
canon-curation pack gains pack-version-bump: a worker that walks the base
branch to each pack's last bump, cuts today's next version for every pack
with a shipping change since, and commits the manifests straight onto main

turns into a run.

instruction to bump by hand or write a VERSIONS.md row. VERSIONS.md becomes

input.title: A pack migration record cannot name the version it lands at now that versions are cut on main
input.body:
Found by the review of #1733 (the `task-cadence-terms` record, `packs/claudinite-tasks/migrations/2026-09-05-task-cadence-terms/migration.mjs`).

A pack migration record carries `version`: the pack version at which its change lands, and `migrationApplies` (`engine/checks/helpers/active-migrations.mjs`) holds the record in a member's gap while `record.version > installed`. The header there says a record "lands in the same change as the bump it names". Since #1726 the bump is cut on `main` by `pack-version-bump` after the merge, so a record in a pull request can no longer name that number: too low (below the pack's current version) and every converged member skips the record — its codemod never runs anywhere, silently; too high and a fully converged member re-applies it every night until the canon passes it.

#1733 writes the next number the bump would cut for the pack as it stands (`60906.5` for a pack at `60906.4`), which holds unless another change to the same pack merges first on the same day. No canon pack has landed a record since #1726, so this is the first record to meet the gap.

The mechanism that closes it belongs to the pack that owns the bump (`claudinite-canon-curation`, `pack-version-bump`): a record may carry a placeholder (`version: 'next'`), the bump stamps it with the number it cuts for that pack in the same commit, and `recordVersion` reads the placeholder as "not yet cut" — `migrationApplies` already falls back to the record's date (`recordDirIsRecent`) when no version can be read, which keeps a not-yet-stamped record applying, idempotently, in the minutes between merge and bump. Pin it with the engine's migrations test and the bump worker's test.

Refs #1725 #1726

Phase 1 of #1725: every scheduler tick asks every task that states a condition, and the task's own `preconditions` carry the whole answer. The engine keeps no scheduling state and no calendar of its own.

## The vocabulary

| term | holds when |
|---|---|
| `due:<daily\|weekly\|monthly>` | no run of the task started or ended since that cadence's most recent anchor on the repo's schedule |
| `last-run-over:<12h\|1d\|7d>` | the task's newest run started more than that long ago, or none in the 40-day horizon |
| `last-run-not-failed` | the task's newest run is not at a failure park — the opt-in that stops a task past its own failure |

`preconditions` is optional. **Absent or empty means the task is not on the schedule**: the scheduler never asks it, and it runs only from an item somebody creates (a mark, a hand-created item, a `--wake`, a chain link, a fan-out target), at whose pick the empty expression holds. A term that reads the item itself (`request-eligible`, `needsItem: true`) keeps its task off the schedule the same way — nothing to judge at a tick. `isScheduledTask(decl, terms)` decides both. The `woken` term the first commit introduced was retired on review: "somebody created my item" is true of every run, so as a precondition it said nothing.

`frequency` and `none` are retired. The contract's door reads a legacy `frequency` as the cadence term it meant (first in `preconditions`, a `none` beside it dropped, the field deleted; `manual` adds no term); `legacy-task-fields` advises the field and `task-declaration-shape` names the edit. The `task-cadence-terms` migration record folds the field into members' own local `task.json` files as anchored text on their nightly update; #1732 retires the door after the window. (#1783 records that a record can no longer name the version the bump cuts on `main`; this record names the next number for the pack as it stands.)

## The mechanism

- A new `runs` signal — the task's own unqualified work items an executor picked, newest first, the item under evaluation excluded — is what the three terms read, and it sets every other signal's window to "since this task's newest run that actually ran" (a rejected item does not move it), falling back to the cadence's period plus an hour with no run in the horizon. **A run begins at the pick**: an item still wearing `blocked` or `waiting-for-executor`, open or closed, is not a run (the simulator found F32: a deduped twin, or a still-waiting sibling, read as this period's run and the survivor declined at its pick).
- The scheduler run asks every scheduled task at every tick. The run-history terms are judged first, over the queue the run already fetched, so a task whose cadence declines collects nothing else; only an undecided ask collects the task's other signals. A yes files a ready planned item, a no is one log line (`asked <task>: no — <reason>`), an ask the scheduler cannot decide fails open. At a pick the executor reads the history only where a term or a windowed collector reads it.
- One live item per task is the engine's only invariant. A parked item (any kind, failure included) is not live: the next occurrence is filed beside it unless the task declares `last-run-not-failed`. The schedule board, the first-window booking, the sleeping-item migration and the engine-owned lane hold are deleted.
- Hand-created items, forced mints and `--wake` stamp `Woken:`; the cadence terms hold on a woken item (the wake stands in for the cadence) while every other condition still applies. `itemFacts` treats any item that is not the scheduler's own unqualified planned item as woken.
- The executor re-evaluates at pick as before, over the item's facts and the repo schedule; a decline still closes the item `rejected`.

Every canon declaration is converted (`daily` → `due:daily`, `weekly` → `due:weekly`, `monthly` → `due:monthly`; the four `manual` tasks carry no `preconditions`; the request implementer carries `["request-eligible"]`). Pack versions are not bumped here — `pack-version-bump` cuts them on `main`.

## What changed where

- `packs/claudinite-tasks/` — `calendar.mjs` (the cadence-term parse, `statesConditions`, `holdsOnFailure`), `precondition-policy.mjs` (the three terms, partial evaluation, `preconditionNeedsItem`, `none` retired), `task-contract.mjs` (the door, `taskCadence`, `isScheduledTask`, `preconditions` optional), `task.schema.json`, the two checks, `signals/` (the `runs` collector and the unpicked rule), `queue/signals.mjs` (the window, the cheap-first seam, the conditional history read), `queue/scheduler-run.mjs` (the stateless run; `schedule-board.mjs` deleted), `queue/executor.mjs`, `queue/work-item.mjs` (`Woken:`, `itemFacts`), `queue/create-work-item.mjs`, `queue/anchors.mjs`, `queue/janitor-rules.mjs`, the new migration record; tests for all of it.
- `engine/migrations/` — the anchored-text `frequency` rewrite (`manual` drops the field, and a list it leaves empty) and its registry op.
- Every pack's `tasks/*/task.json`, and the per-pack tests and READMEs that named `frequency`.
- `packs/claudinite-dashboard/` — the roster reads the cadence off `preconditions`, an empty expression as unscheduled and an unreadable one as unknown; a failure park reads as a held lane only where the declaration says `last-run-not-failed`.
- `packs/claudinite-tasks/test/sim/` and `docs/tasks-dispatch/SCENARIOS.md` — the simulator models the stateless run as the engine writes it; board scenarios retired, S65–S73 ported, S74–S78 added.
- `docs/tasks-dispatch/DESIGN.md` §5 rewritten and §15.33 recorded with the retrospective brief; `docs/task-preconditions/DESIGN.md`; the `writing-tasks` skill.

Reviewed by a code-review pass over the whole diff; its findings are the four commits after the retirement.

Closes #1731

All three items are done and pushed to [PR #1733](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1733), which is rebased on `main` (eleven commits) with the full suite green (3274 tests) and both repo checks clean.

**The correction, taken as you meant it.** The `woken` term is retired. A precondition says what must hold of the world or of the run history; "somebody created my item" holds of every run, so the term said nothing. A declaration now says the same thing by stating nothing: `preconditions` is optional, and absent or empty means the task is off the schedule. The scheduler never asks it and it runs only from an item somebody creates, at whose pick the empty expression holds. The one wrinkle is the built-in request implementer, whose real condition `request-eligible` is about the item itself. Its term now declares `needsItem`, which keeps that task off the schedule too, since there is nothing to judge at a tick. `deploy-oauth-exchange`, `fleet-baseline`, `adopt-requested-packs` and `verify-production` carry no `preconditions` key at all.

**Merge conflicts.** Main's #1734 had rewritten fifteen of the same test files. I took main's versions and re-applied only the run-history plumbing they now need.

**The review.** I ran the code-review pass at high effort over the whole branch diff. It confirmed the two-pass ask, the terms, the unpicked rule, the `Woken:` stamping and the text rewriter as sound, and raised six findings. Four are fixed in the last four commits:

- The migration record's version sat below the pack's current version, so no converged member would ever have run the `frequency` rewrite. Fixed to the next number the bump cuts. This is a gap in the bump-on-main process for any future record, filed as [#1783](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1783).
- `create-work-item` judged "scheduled" without the task's terms, so it would have refused an unqualified item for the request implementer.
- The executor paged the whole 40-day issue list at every pick of an item-only task. It now reads the history only where a term or a windowed collector reads it, pinned by a test.
- Stale `woken` and `frequency` wording in the schema, the policy header and two comments.

Two I left as they are: the simulator re-implements the three terms rather than calling the engine's evaluator, which the sim's author did deliberately to model the writes, and I would rather you decide whether that harness should couple to the engine. The remaining advisory findings are the dashboard's existing cross-pack reaches, unchanged in kind.

Folders the review pass touched (non-test):

```
packs/claudinite-tasks/           calendar (statesConditions), precondition-policy (needsItem read, woken term gone), task-contract (preconditions optional, terms-aware isScheduledTask), schema, the two checks, scheduler-run, executor, signals (conditional history read), create-work-item, the migration record's version, implement-request's term and declaration
engine/migrations/                the text rewriter drops `manual` to no expression
packs/*/tasks/*/task.json         the four manual tasks lose their preconditions key
packs/claudinite-dashboard/       model, board: empty expression reads as unscheduled, unreadable as unknown
docs/, writing-tasks skill        the retired term purged, §15.33 records the retirement
```

> ⚠️ Still open: your review of PR #1733 ("lgtm" merges); the simulator-coupling question above; after merge, the verification and retrospective sub-issues of #1725 and #1732's `Blocked-by`.

1	---
2	name: writing-handover-issues
3	description: How to write a task list a PERSON will execute — a handover issue, an adoption checklist, a "steps only a human can do" list. Use when filing or editing any issue whose body asks a human to click, set, register or copy something. Not for issues describing work you will do yourself.
4	metadata:
5	  force-load-on-tool-calls:
6	    - 'mcp__github__issue_write.body /- \[ \]/'
7	---
8	
9	# Writing a task for a human
10	
11	An issue you will act on is a *description*. An issue a **person** will act on is an
12	*instrument*: they open it with the settings page in the next tab, and every word that is
13	not the next click is in the way. The two are written differently, and the second one is
14	almost always written like the first.
15	
16	The failure is not being wrong. It is being **complete** — the reader skims, loses the
17	thread, and does three of six steps.
18	
19	## The body has exactly two parts, in this order
20	
21	1. **The checklist.** Checkboxes and nothing else. No prose between them, no italic
22	   asides under them, no notes about what breaks. A reader must be able to work top to
23	   bottom without their eye leaving the boxes.
24	2. **Everything else, below it.** Why the task exists, what each step buys, what stays
25	   broken while it is undone, background, links to the design. All of it, after the
26	   last checkbox, under its own heading.
27	
28	One or two sentences may sit *above* the checklist to say what the issue is for. Not
29	more. If you find yourself explaining a step, you are writing part 2 — move it down.
30	
31	Splitting them is the whole skill. The information the corpus asks a handover to carry
32	— what breaks while each step is off — still has to be there; it just has to be
33	somewhere the person executing is not reading.
34	
35	## One step, one line, one action
36	
37	A checkbox is an **imperative** naming one thing to do:
38	
39	> - [ ] Set the repository variable `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` → [Variables](https://github.com/o/r/settings/variables/actions)
40	
41	Not `You will need to set…`, not a step that also explains, not a step that is really
42	two. If a step needs a second sentence, either it is two steps or that sentence is
43	background. If it needs a paragraph, it is a sub-issue.
44	
45	Bold nothing inside a step. Emphasis on every line is emphasis on none, and these lines
46	are already the only thing in their section.
47	
48	## Link the screen, don't describe the path
49	
50	Every step that happens in a UI carries **the deepest URL that lands on that screen**,
51	as the step's own link. Never a breadcrumb trail — `Settings → Secrets and variables →
52	Actions → Variables` is four things to get right and a link is zero.
53	
54	Substitute the real owner and repo into the URL; a template with `<owner>` in it is a
55	breadcrumb wearing a link's clothes. Open every link, or construct it from a page you
56	have actually seen — a settings URL that 404s costs more than the trail you replaced.
57	
58	## Getting a value: say where on the screen it is
59	
60	The step that *produces* a value is the one that goes wrong, because the writer knows
61	the page and the reader does not. Name, in the words that appear on that screen:
62	
63	- the control that mints or reveals it — *"press Generate a new client secret"*
64	- where the value then appears — *"the value shown once, under Client secrets"*
65	- what it looks like, when that disambiguates — *"begins `Iv23`"*, *"a 32-character hex
66	  string"*
67	- if it is shown once, say so **in that step**. That is not an explanation; it is part
68	  of the action.
69	
70	> - [ ] Copy the **Client ID** — [App settings](https://github.com/settings/apps/x), top of the page under the app name
71	
72	A value produced by one step and consumed by another is named identically in both, so
73	the reader can find what to paste.
74	
75	## Order so that every step is doable when it is reached
76	
77	Walk the list as the reader: at each box, does everything it needs already exist? A step
78	asking for a value a later step mints is the most common defect, and it reads perfectly
79	to the author.
80	
81	Then close the gaps. A step that **mints or reveals a value** and the step that
82	**pastes it where it lives** are one pair, and they go immediately after each other —
83	never a block of producers followed later by a block of consumers, however tidily each
84	block groups by screen. Every box between them is a value the reader is holding in
85	their head while doing something else, and one that is shown once is held there at the
86	price of minting it again. Pair by pair beats phase by phase even when it means opening
87	the same screen twice.
88	
89	That pairing is what keeps the value out of the reader's head, so it is also the reason
90	the list needs no note reminding them to hold it.
91	
92	## Drop the steps that are not steps
93	
94	A box that is usually a no-op teaches the reader to skim exactly the list that exists to
95	stop them skimming. If the honest answer for most readers is "nothing to do", it is
96	background, or it is a decision stated once above the list — not a checkbox.
97	
98	## Close with one observable
99	
100	End the issue with the single thing the person can look at to know they are done, in
101	what they will see rather than what will be true. Not "sign-in works" — *"loading the
102	page signed out shows Sign in with GitHub, and clicking it returns you signed in"*.
103	
104	## Before you file
105	
106	- Read only the checkboxes, in order. Can a person who has never seen this repo do
107	  them? That is the artifact; everything else is the appendix.
108	- Count the words in the longest box. If it is over about fifteen, it is carrying an
109	  explanation.
110	- Confirm each link resolves and each named control still has that name.
111	
112	## Where this applies
113	
114	Any issue whose body asks a person to click, set, register, install or copy: the
115	human-only handover basics requires, a pack's `adoptionHandover` rendered into an issue,
116	a migration's out-of-band setup phase, a production verification someone else will run.
117	The rule that such work gets **its own issue** rather than a note in a PR body is
118	basics' *Handing over a step only a human can perform*; this is how that issue is
119	written.

   bottom without their eye leaving the boxes.
2. **Everything else, below it.** Why the task exists, what each step buys, what stays
   broken while it is undone, background, links to the design. All of it, after the
   last checkbox, under its own heading.

One or two sentences may sit *above* the checklist to say what the issue is for. Not
more. If you find yourself explaining a step, you are writing part 2 — move it down.

Splitting them is the whole skill. The information the corpus asks a handover to carry
— what breaks while each step is off — still has to be there; it just has to be
somewhere the person executing is not reading.

## One step, one line, one action

A checkbox is an **imperative** naming one thing to do:

> - [ ] Set the repository variable `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` → [Variables](https://github.com/o/r/settings/variables/actions)

Not `You will need to set…`, not a step that also explains, not a step that is really
two. If a step needs a second sentence, either it is two steps or that sentence is
background. If it needs a paragraph, it is a sub-issue.

Bold nothing inside a step. Emphasis on every line is emphasis on none, and these lines
are already the only thing in their section.

## Link the screen, don't describe the path

Every step that happens in a UI carries **the deepest URL that lands on that screen**,
as the step's own link. Never a breadcrumb trail — `Settings → Secrets and variables →
Actions → Variables` is four things to get right and a link is zero.

Substitute the real owner and repo into the URL; a template with `<owner>` in it is a
breadcrumb wearing a link's clothes. Open every link, or construct it from a page you
have actually seen — a settings URL that 404s costs more than the trail you replaced.

## Getting a value: say where on the screen it is

The step that *produces* a value is the one that goes wrong, because the writer knows
the page and the reader does not. Name, in the words that appear on that screen:

- the control that mints or reveals it — *"press Generate a new client secret"*
- where the value then appears — *"the value shown once, under Client secrets"*
- what it looks like, when that disambiguates — *"begins `Iv23`"*, *"a 32-character hex
  string"*
- if it is shown once, say so **in that step**. That is not an explanation; it is part
  of the action.

> - [ ] Copy the **Client ID** — [App settings](https://github.com/settings/apps/x), top of the page under the app name

A value produced by one step and consumed by another is named identically in both, so
the reader can find what to paste.

## Order so that every step is doable when it is reached

Walk the list as the reader: at each box, does everything it needs already exist? A step
asking for a value a later step mints is the most common defect, and it reads perfectly
to the author.

Then close the gaps. A step that **mints or reveals a value** and the step that
**pastes it where it lives** are one pair, and they go immediately after each other —
never a block of producers followed later by a block of consumers, however tidily each
block groups by screen. Every box between them is a value the reader is holding in
their head while doing something else, and one that is shown once is held there at the
price of minting it again. Pair by pair beats phase by phase even when it means opening
the same screen twice.

That pairing is what keeps the value out of the reader's head, so it is also the reason
the list needs no note reminding them to hold it.

## Drop the steps that are not steps

A box that is usually a no-op teaches the reader to skim exactly the list that exists to
stop them skimming. If the honest answer for most readers is "nothing to do", it is
background, or it is a decision stated once above the list — not a checkbox.

## Close with one observable

End the issue with the single thing the person can look at to know they are done, in
what they will see rather than what will be true. Not "sign-in works" — *"loading the
page signed out shows Sign in with GitHub, and clicking it returns you signed in"*.

## Before you file

- Read only the checkboxes, in order. Can a person who has never seen this repo do
  them? That is the artifact; everything else is the appendix.
- Count the words in the longest box. If it is over about fifteen, it is carrying an
  explanation.
- Confirm each link resolves and each named control still has that name.

## Where this applies

Any issue whose body asks a person to click, set, register, install or copy: the
human-only handover basics requires, a pack's `adoptionHandover` rendered into an issue,
a migration's out-of-band setup phase, a production verification someone else will run.
The rule that such work gets **its own issue** rather than a note in a PR body is
basics' *Handing over a step only a human can perform*; this is how that issue is
written.

{"number":1755,"title":"Move the task design docs under packs/claudinite-tasks/docs, kept out of the vendor set","body":"Blocked-by: #1733
Automerge: anything

<!-- filed by /do-later -->

Move every task-related design doc out of the repo-level `docs/` into the pack that owns the subject, `packs/claudinite-tasks/docs/`, and make sure members never receive them.

## The move

`git mv` these four directories whole, keeping each directory's name and every file's content — the historical records among them (`per-project-scheduling/MIGRATION.md`, `task-code-work/check-fix-subsumption-audit.md`) are moved, never rewritten:

- `docs/tasks-dispatch/` → `packs/claudinite-tasks/docs/tasks-dispatch/`
- `docs/task-preconditions/` → `packs/claudinite-tasks/docs/task-preconditions/`
- `docs/task-code-work/` → `packs/claudinite-tasks/docs/task-code-work/`
- `docs/per-project-scheduling/` → `packs/claudinite-tasks/docs/per-project-scheduling/`

Everything else under `docs/` (`declarative-checks`, `versioned-updates`, `skill-usage-metrics`, `website-release-flows`, `conversion-inventory.md`, `future-directions.md`) is not task-related and stays.

## Keep them out of the vendor set

A pack's vendor set is its whole directory today (`isPackFile` in `packs/claudinite-lifecycle/updates/pack-update.mjs`: `rel.startsWith('packs/<id>/')`), so the moved docs would reach every member on the next converge. Carve a pack's `docs/` out of what vendors. Decide whether the carve-out is generic (no pack's `docs/` vendors — `packs/claudinite-dashboard/docs/` exists and is reached from the dashboard's own README; say in the PR whether members are meant to receive it) or scoped to `claudinite-tasks`, and say which in the PR body. Pin it with a test against the real canon tree: the pack's `docs/` directory stays out, and an operational sibling directory of the same pack still vendors — assert the whole containing directory, not one file.

The `.claudinite-settings.json` barrier `siblings: packs → to: docs` exists because `docs/` is outside the vendor set, so a pack file's reference to it resolves to nothing in a consumer. Once `packs/claudinite-tasks/docs/` is outside it too, the same premise holds for a pack file that references it — extend that barrier (through the baseline pack's `config.barriers`, never standalone code) so a pack file citing `packs/claudinite-tasks/docs/` by path is judged the same way, and keep citing the docs by `§` name from code comments, as they are cited today.

## Sweep the references

- `.claudinite-settings.json`: the two `reference-integrity` waivers whose `path` is `docs/task-code-work/` and `docs/per-project-scheduling/` — re-point the paths, keep the reasons.
- `README.md`: the `docs/per-project-scheduling/DESIGN.md` link.
- `packs/claudinite-tasks/test/sim/coverage.test.mjs`: the relative path it reads `DESIGN.md` from.
- `packs/claudinite-tasks/test/queue/narrow-diff.test.mjs`: a `docs/tasks-dispatch/DESIGN.md` fixture string — a classification fixture, fine to leave or re-point.
- Inside the moved docs: relative links out to `../../packs/…` and `../../engine/…` change depth (the docs sit two directories deeper); links between the four moved docs survive as they are. Run the repo's reference-integrity check rather than grepping by hand.
- The `§`-named citations in code and prose (`tasks-dispatch DESIGN §5`, `per-project-scheduling DESIGN §1`, …) name no path and need nothing.

## Done when

- `git ls-files docs/` lists none of the four directories, and `git ls-files packs/claudinite-tasks/docs/` lists all of them.
- The vendor-set test proves `packs/claudinite-tasks/docs/` is excluded and the pack's operational directories still vendor.
- `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` is green; `node engine/checks/check_the_work.mjs --changed --base origin/main` and `node engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs` report no blocking finding.

Owner ruling: `Automerge: anything` — the run lands itself whatever its diff contains.

{"number":1774,"title":"Per-pack task tests assert the pack's own code, not the task mechanism","body":"Blocked-by: #1755
Automerge: test-changes

<!-- filed by /do-later -->

Owner ruling: a test belongs to the code it exercises. A pack's test of one of its tasks proves that pack's own code — its task-local `preconditions.mjs` terms, its workers, its declared merge-rules classes, and any genuinely intricate use of the mechanism (a composed `||` expression the pack designed, a `schedule_after` chain, a fan-out) — never that the task mechanism runs a plain declaration: nothing is learned from asserting that `due:weekly` parses as a weekly cadence, that a built-in term declares the signal it reads, or that a declaration validates. The mechanism's own suite (`packs/claudinite-tasks/test/`) proves the mechanism once, for every declaration.

## The sweep

Read every `packs/*/test/` test whose subject is a task declaration — today `chrome-extension/test/tasks.test.mjs`, `claudinite-canon-curation/test/tasks.test.mjs`, `claudinite-growth/test/tasks.test.mjs`, `claudinite-lifecycle/test/tasks.test.mjs`, and any sibling in `basics`, `claudinite-fleet-sheepdog`, `product-wiki`, `tidy-repo`, `claudinite-dashboard` whose name or body names a task — and in each:

- **Delete** assertions that re-run the mechanism over the declaration: `taskCadence(decl)` equalling the term the file states; `preconditionSignals(...)` equalling the built-ins' signal list; `validateTaskDeclaration(decl)` being empty (the `task-declaration-shape` check judges every declaration over the real tree already); `evaluatePrecondition` driven only to show a built-in run-history or movement term holds or declines; and every self-pin of a declared literal (`agent_model`, `expected_outcome`, `automerge`, `invocation_endpoint`, `code_work_timeout` equalling what the file says).
- **Keep, and where thin, strengthen** what proves the pack's own code: a task-local term's decisions over fabricated signals (which members a fleet term selects, that an unproven fleet state errors rather than reading as nothing), a worker's behaviour, a merge-rules class's verdicts over file lists, and a two-artifact claim that could drift (a worker file the declaration names exists; a workflow runs the worker the declaration names).
- **Keep** a mechanism assertion only where the usage is intricate — the composition is the pack's design, not the term's — and say so in the test's comment in one line.
- A test file left with nothing of the pack's own to prove is deleted whole; a pack-level roster test ("the pack keeps exactly these tasks") stays only where it pins a two-artifact claim (a catalog row, a README table) and not the directory listing to itself.

`packs/claudinite-tasks/test/` is the mechanism's own suite and is out of scope: there, the mechanism is the code under test.

## Write the rule down

Add one bullet to `packs/basics/skills/writing-tests/SKILL.md`, beside the "Never pin a declaration to itself" bullet, stating the ruling above in the skill's own register: a test proves the code it belongs to, not the mechanism it uses; a mechanism assertion in a consumer's test earns its place only for intricate usage, named in the test. One sentence, near forty words, no restatement of the sweep.

## Done when

- Every kept assertion in the swept files reads as a claim about that pack's own code or an intricate usage named as such.
- `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` is green with the suite's test count lower, not higher; `node engine/checks/check_the_work.mjs --changed --base origin/main` and `node engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs` report no blocking finding.
- The PR body lists, per pack, how many tests were removed and which were kept as intricate usage.

{"number":1783,"title":"A pack migration record cannot name the version it lands at now that versions are cut on main","body":"Found by the review of #1733 (the `task-cadence-terms` record, `packs/claudinite-tasks/migrations/2026-09-05-task-cadence-terms/migration.mjs`).

A pack migration record carries `version`: the pack version at which its change lands, and `migrationApplies` (`engine/checks/helpers/active-migrations.mjs`) holds the record in a member's gap while `record.version > installed`. The header there says a record "lands in the same change as the bump it names". Since #1726 the bump is cut on `main` by `pack-version-bump` after the merge, so a record in a pull request can no longer name that number: too low (below the pack's current version) and every converged member skips the record — its codemod never runs anywhere, silently; too high and a fully converged member re-applies it every night until the canon passes it.

#1733 writes the next number the bump would cut for the pack as it stands (`60906.5` for a pack at `60906.4`), which holds unless another change to the same pack merges first on the same day. No canon pack has landed a record since #1726, so this is the first record to meet the gap.

The mechanism that closes it belongs to the pack that owns the bump (`claudinite-canon-curation`, `pack-version-bump`): a record may carry a placeholder (`version: 'next'`), the bump stamps it with the number it cuts for that pack in the same commit, and `recordVersion` reads the placeholder as "not yet cut" — `migrationApplies` already falls back to the record's date (`recordDirIsRecent`) when no version can be read, which keeps a not-yet-stamped record applying, idempotently, in the minutes between merge and bump. Pin it with the engine's migrations test and the bump worker's test.

#1733 writes the next number the bump would cut for the pack as it stands (`60906.5` for a pack at `60906.4`), which holds unless another change to the same pack merges first on the same day. No canon pack has landed a record since #1726, so this is the first record to meet the gap.

The mechanism that closes it belongs to the pack that owns the bump (`claudinite-canon-curation`, `pack-version-bump`): a record may carry a placeholder (`version: 'next'`), the bump stamps it with the number it cuts for that pack in the same commit, and `recordVersion` reads the placeholder as "not yet cut" — `migrationApplies` already falls back to the record's date (`recordDirIsRecent`) when no version can be read, which keeps a not-yet-stamped record applying, idempotently, in the minutes between merge and bump. Pin it with the engine's migrations test and the bump worker's test.

{"number":1725,"title":"Scheduling as preconditions: retire `frequency` and the schedule board","body":"## Problem

The scheduler is opaque and keeps state. A task's "when" is split between an engine-owned calendar (`frequency`, anchors, the schedule board's watermark, the first-window booking, the lane a failure park holds) and the task-owned `preconditions`. The engine decides exactly-once-per-period semantics on the task's behalf, and every piece of that state is something that can go stale, be mangled, or confuse a renamed task.

## The decision (owner, 2026-09-05)

Every tick asks every task, and the task's own preconditions carry the whole answer. The engine keeps no scheduling state and no calendar of its own:

- The cadence is a precondition term read off the task's own run history — both shapes available: `due:<daily|weekly|monthly>` (anchored on the repo's `taskScheduler` schedule) and `last-run-over:<duration>` (elapsed).
- The first-sight rule (a just-adopted task never runs off-anchor) is dropped outright.
- Whether a failed run stops the next one is the task's to say, explicitly — `last-run-not-failed` — and is not even a default.
- `woken` is the spelling of "runs only when someone asks" (the retired `frequency: manual`).
- The schedule board is deleted. A decline is a log line; the next tick asks again.

The end state and its rationale are in `docs/tasks-dispatch/DESIGN.md` §5 (rewritten) and decision §15.33, with the vocabulary in `docs/task-preconditions/DESIGN.md`.

## Plan

- [ ] **Phase 1 — one PR.** The vocabulary (`due:`, `last-run-over:`, `last-run-not-failed`, `woken`; `none` retired), the `runs` signal and the since-last-run window, cheap-first evaluation (run-history terms judged before any other signal is collected), the scheduler run without board, first-sight booking or lane hold (one live item per task is the only invariant), `Woken:` stamped on forced and hand-created items, the `frequency` door with its `legacy-task-fields` advisory, the nightly update rewriting members' own task files, the 26 canon declarations, the dashboard, the simulator and the docs. Predicted diff: `packs/claudinite-tasks/` (queue, signals, contract, checks, tests, sim), every pack's `tasks/*/task.json`, `packs/claudinite-dashboard/`, `packs/claudinite-growth/skills/writing-tasks/`, `docs/`. Policy `nothing` — the design's first render. Exit: merged on `main`.
- [ ] **Phase 2 — verify in production** (link filed at the merge, per verify-in-production): the canon's scheduler runs after the merge show every declared task asked at each tick, declines as log lines only, an item filed only on a yes, and no write to a `[claudinite-schedule]` issue.
- [ ] **Phase 3 — retire the tolerances** (link, `Not-before:` two weeks past the merge): drop the `frequency` door and the `none` acceptance once the nightly update has had its window to rewrite members' own task files.
- [ ] **Phase 4 — retrospective** (link filed at the merge, ripe a week after it): the brief is in the design.

Human gates expected: one, the phase 1 review.

input.body:
Phase 1 divergences from the plan above (2026-09-06, on the review of #1733):

- **The `woken` term is retired.** The plan spelled "runs only when someone asks" as a `woken` precondition; on review the owner ruled it redundant — "somebody created my item" is true of every run, so as a precondition it says nothing. A declaration now says the same thing by stating no `preconditions` at all: absent or empty means the task is off the schedule and runs only from an item somebody creates. A term that reads the item itself (`request-eligible`, `needsItem`) keeps its task off the schedule the same way. Three run-history terms remain. DESIGN §15.33 carries the dated note.
- **A run begins at the pick (F32).** The simulator port found that a deduped twin, or a still-waiting sibling, read as this period's run at the survivor's pick, so the occurrence was spent with nothing run. The `runs` collector now drops any item still wearing a pre-pick status, open or closed. SCENARIOS.md ledger, F32.
- **The migration record's version** cannot name the number the bump cuts on `main` (#1726); the record names the next number for the pack as it stands, and the process gap is #1783.

Phase 1's PR is #1733, rebased on `main` and under review.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files, comment-only changes, and history-keeping updates (a version bump, a changelog or `VERSIONS.md` row).
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

2. **Key Technical Concepts:**

   - **Stateless scheduler run**: every tick asks every scheduled task through its own `preconditions`; yes → READY planned item; no → one log line (`asked <task>: no — <reason>`); undecidable → fail open. No schedule board, no first-window booking, no engine lane hold. One invariant: one live item per task (`LIVE_STATUSES`); parks are not live.
   - **Run-history terms** reading the `runs` signal: `due:<daily|weekly|monthly>`, `last-run-over:<Nh|Nd>`, `last-run-not-failed`. The `woken` term was retired mid-session on the owner's correction.
   - **`preconditions` optional**: absent or empty means the task is not on the schedule — it runs only from an item somebody creates (mark, hand-created item, `--wake`, chain link, fan-out target), at whose pick the empty expression holds. `isScheduledTask(decl, terms)` = `statesConditions(preconditions) && !preconditionNeedsItem(preconditions, terms)`.
   - **`needsItem`**: a term declaring it (only `request-eligible`) reads the item itself, so there is nothing to judge at a tick — its task is off the schedule.
   - **A run begins at the pick (F32)**: an item still wearing `blocked` or `waiting-for-executor` (open, or closed beside a terminal label the scheduler's dedupe/orphan/supersede writes add) was never picked and is not in the task's run history.
   - **`Woken:` body field** stamped by `createWorkItem`, `wakeItem`, forced mint; `itemFacts(item).woken` = stamped || not (unqualified title && origin !== ad-hoc). Unchanged by the woken-term retirement — cadence terms still hold on a woken item.

     // Whether the declaration states any condition at all. Absent or empty, the task
     // is off the schedule: the scheduler never asks it, and it runs only from an item
     // somebody created — at whose pick an empty expression holds.
     export const statesConditions = (preconditions) => entriesOf(preconditions).some((alts) => alts.length > 0);

     const gatesOn = (preconditions, term) =>
       entriesOf(preconditions).some((alts) => alts.length === 1 && alts[0].name === term && alts[0].arg === null);
     export const holdsOnFailure = (preconditions) => gatesOn(preconditions, NOT_FAILED_TERM);

       const parsed = parsePreconditions(preconditions);
       if (parsed.kind !== 'conditions') return false;

---
name: committing
description: How a commit is cut — one concern per commit, the issue it references, a landed commit revised only by a new one, files staged by name. Use before any git commit.
metadata:
  force-load-on-tool-calls:
    - 'Bash.command /(^|[;&|]\s*|\n\s*)git\s+commit\b/'
---

# Committing

- **One concern per commit.** If two changes could each stand alone, split them; a message that
  wants numbered items is the split talking.
- **Reference the issue** — `Refs #n`, or `Fixes #n` / `Closes #n` where the commit finishes it;
  the `task-lifecycle` check reads it off the branch.
- **A landed commit is revised by a new commit**, never a rewrite of that one.
- **Stage by name** — `git add <paths>` for the files this commit is about; `-a` sweeps in whatever
  else was in progress.

---
name: running-the-suite
description: Running this repo's test suite — the one command that covers it, reading a run's output from a file instead of re-running it, iterating on the tests an edit touches, and staging a new test file before certifying a run. Use before any node --test.
metadata:
  force-load-on-tool-calls:
    - 'Bash.command /\bnode\s+--test\b/'
---

# Running the suite

- **The whole suite is one command** — `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`. There is no test
  script, `node --test <dir>` does not recurse, and a bash glob without `globstar` reached 37 of 65
  files; `ci.yml`'s array is not authoritative.
- **Read a run's output from a file** — redirect one run and grep that file for the slice you need;
  never re-run the ~55s suite to re-slice unchanged output. (1)
- **`git add` a new test file before certifying a run green** — `git ls-files` excludes an unstaged
  file, so the run never executed it; the `untracked-test-file` finding at Stop says which. (2)
- **Iterating on a sweep across many files** — run only the test files the edit touches, plus
  `check_the_work`; spend the whole suite and `check_the_world` once, at the end. Both are
  whole-tree aggregates whose verdict cannot turn on one file. (3)

---
name: writing-handover-issues
description: How to write a task list a PERSON will execute — a handover issue, an adoption checklist, a "steps only a human can do" list. Use when filing or editing any issue whose body asks a human to click, set, register or copy something. Not for issues describing work you will do yourself.
metadata:
  force-load-on-tool-calls:
    - 'mcp__github__issue_write.body /- \[ \]/'
---

# Writing a task for a human

An issue you will act on is a *description*. An issue a **person** will act on is an
*instrument*: they open it with the settings page in the next tab, and every word that is
not the next click is in the way. The two are written differently, and the second one is
almost always written like the first.

The failure is not being wrong. It is being **complete** — the reader skims, loses the
thread, and does three of six steps.

## The body has exactly two parts, in this order

1. **The checklist.** Checkboxes and nothing else. No prose between them, no italic
   asides under them, no notes about what breaks. A reader must be able to work top to
   bottom without their eye leaving the boxes.
2. **Everything else, below it.** Why the task exists, what each step buys, what stays
   broken while it is undone, background, links to the design. All of it, after the
   last checkbox, under its own heading.

One or two sentences may sit *above* the checklist to say what the issue is for. Not
more. If you find yourself explaining a step, you are writing part 2 — move it down.

Splitting them is the whole skill. The information the corpus asks a handover to carry
— what breaks while each step is off — still has to be there; it just has to be
somewhere the person executing is not reading.

## One step, one line, one action

A checkbox is an **imperative** naming one thing to do:

> - [ ] Set the repository variable `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` → [Variables](https://github.com/o/r/settings/variables/actions)

Not `You will need to set…`, not a step that also explains, not a step that is really
two. If a step needs a second sentence, either it is two steps or that sentence is
background. If it needs a paragraph, it is a sub-issue.

Bold nothing inside a step. Emphasis on every line is emphasis on none, and these lines
are already the only thing in their section.

## Link the screen, don't describe the path

Every step that happens in a UI carries **the deepest URL that lands on that screen**,
as the step's own link. Never a breadcrumb trail — `Settings → Secrets and variables →
Actions → Variables` is four things to get right and a link is zero.

Substitute the real owner and repo into the URL; a template with `<owner>` in it is a
breadcrumb wearing a link's clothes. Open every link, or construct it from a page you
have actually seen — a settings URL that 404s costs more than the trail you replaced.

## Getting a value: say where on the screen it is

The step that *produces* a value is the one that goes wrong, because the writer knows
the page and the reader does not. Name, in the words that appear on that screen:

- the control that mints or reveals it — *"press Generate a new client secret"*
- where the value then appears — *"the value shown once, under Client secrets"*
- what it looks like, when that disambiguates — *"begins `Iv23`"*, *"a 32-character hex
  string"*
- if it is shown once, say so **in that step**. That is not an explanation; it is part
  of the action.

> - [ ] Copy the **Client ID** — [App settings](https://github.com/settings/apps/x), top of the page under the app name

A value produced by one step and consumed by another is named identically in both, so
the reader can find what to paste.

## Order so that every step is doable when it is reached

Walk the list as the reader: at each box, does everything it needs already exist? A step
asking for a value a later step mints is the most common defect, and it reads perfectly
to the author.

Then close the gaps. A step that **mints or reveals a value** and the step that
**pastes it where it lives** are one pair, and they go immediately after each other —
never a block of producers followed later by a block of consumers, however tidily each
block groups by screen. Every box between them is a value the reader is holding in
their head while doing something else, and one that is shown once is held there at the
price of minting it again. Pair by pair beats phase by phase even when it means opening
the same screen twice.

That pairing is what keeps the value out of the reader's head, so it is also the reason
the list needs no note reminding them to hold it.

## Drop the steps that are not steps

A box that is usually a no-op teaches the reader to skim exactly the list that exists to
stop them skimming. If the honest answer for most readers is "nothing to do", it is
background, or it is a decision stated once above the list — not a checkbox.

## Close with one observable

End the issue with the single thing the person can look at to know they are done, in
what they will see rather than what will be true. Not "sign-in works" — *"loading the
page signed out shows Sign in with GitHub, and clicking it returns you signed in"*.

## Before you file

- Read only the checkboxes, in order. Can a person who has never seen this repo do
  them? That is the artifact; everything else is the appendix.
- Count the words in the longest box. If it is over about fifteen, it is carrying an
  explanation.
- Confirm each link resolves and each named control still has that name.

## Where this applies

Any issue whose body asks a person to click, set, register, install or copy: the
human-only handover basics requires, a pack's `adoptionHandover` rendered into an issue,
a migration's out-of-band setup phase, a production verification someone else will run.
The rule that such work gets **its own issue** rather than a note in a PR body is
basics' *Handing over a step only a human can perform*; this is how that issue is
written.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/writing-claudinite-skills

# Writing Claudinite skills

A corpus skill is a harness-matched trigger (frontmatter `name` + a tight `description`, plus `force-load-on-file-edits-paths` under `metadata` where an edit of the files it names must not start without it — the PreToolUse guard holds such an edit until the skill is loaded; never the harness's `paths`, which limits when the skill is offered at all) plus the body the agent needs at usage time — well under 500 lines, and nothing a deterministic mechanism could carry instead (the promotion ladder in [engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md) decides). A skill may own the rules that validate its action — `checks.mjs` beside the SKILL.md, one module per rule, with their fixture tests under the owning pack's `test/` mirroring the skill's path; shape and the relevance-first gate in [engine/checks/README.md](../../../../engine/checks/README.md#adding-a-rule). Ownership is placement: the skill lives in exactly one owning pack's `skills/` — there is no skill catalog; the pack's own README names what it bundles. Instruction-writing *quality* — how agents actually follow docs — is [authoring-agent-docs](../../../basics/skills/authoring-agent-docs/SKILL.md)' turf; this skill is the corpus mechanics. (1)

skills.name: writing-pack-prose
skills.content:
Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/writing-pack-prose

# Writing pack prose

Whether a candidate *qualifies* as a rule at all, and which mechanism carries it, is
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)'s call — settle it there before writing.

**Start from the foundation:** read the "Write each rule" section of
[authoring-agent-docs](../../../basics/skills/authoring-agent-docs/SKILL.md) first — its
principles (concrete enough to verify, motivation stated, what to do rather than what not to,
the right altitude, emphasis reserved) bind pack prose too. This skill is the pack-specific
layer on top of them, and doesn't restate them.

## The ration

Every rule in a `RULES.md` is paid for by every session in every repo that declares the pack,
forever, whether or not it ever applies — so prose is rationed, and the ration is small.

- **One sentence per rule, near 40 words**: the trigger, the directive, and a consequence
  clause only where the rule cannot be applied without it. A candidate that needs a paragraph
  to land has not been understood well enough to be a rule yet.
- **An extraction pass adds at most two rules.** If more candidates clear the bar, write the
  two strongest and drop the rest — they will recur if they were real.
- **Split a rule that carries two situations.** Each situation is its own rule with its own
  trigger.
- A `SKILL.md` loads only when its activity is under way, so it may carry procedure at length —
  but it is still rationed by the same test: every line must change what the reader does.
  Method, steps and decision points belong there; anything a session must know *without*
  loading it belongs in `RULES.md` or a check, and rationale belongs in the references doc
  below.
- **Moving a rule out of `RULES.md` into a skill** — only where the skill's
  `force-load-on-file-edits-paths` covers *every* moment the rule is needed. A skill whose only
  trigger is its description is picked by the model, not the harness, so a rule that must fire at
  a moment no file edit predicts stays prose, however activity-shaped it reads. (2)

## Shape a rule so it fires

- **Keying a rule to its trigger** — open with the act the reader is performing, not the state
  of the world the rule applies to. Nobody notices that "a value is unknown"; they notice they
  are writing an encoder. A rule keyed to a state never fires, because nothing brings the
  reader to it.
- **Keying a rule the reader reaches while debugging** — name the symptom that sends them
  looking ("A fetch to a host you listed failing in-browser"), not the act that caused it. By
  the time the rule is wanted the act is over, and the symptom is what they can see.
- **Keying a rule that corrects a misconception** — name what the reader wants ("Wanting
  `import`/`export` in extension code"), not the wrong move they might make ("Reaching for a
  bundler"). Someone who doesn't yet know the move is wrong won't recognise themselves in it.
- **Phrasing that trigger** — use the words the reader would use for the situation, and put
  them first and in bold, so the rule is findable by scanning the left margin alone.
- **Choosing the unit** — one block per situation, not one bullet per rule. A reader arrives
  holding a problem, so give them the whole decision in one place rather than a cross-reference
  to three neighbouring bullets.
- **Splitting a rule that only makes sense after the one above it** — don't. If the subject
  needs a "that" pointing back ("Writing that record"), it is a clause of the rule above, not a
  situation of its own. Split when a reader could arrive at the second rule without the first.
- **Separating the blocks** — one blank line between rules. The block is what a reader lands on,
  and an unbroken run of bullets makes them scan lines instead; the separation costs one token.
- **Ordering a file of many rules** — past roughly fifteen, group them under headings naming the
  surface each concerns, so a reader scans headings before subjects. A flat list that long makes
  every bold subject do the work one heading would.
- **Grouping that separates two rules which qualify each other** — add an explicit pointer from
  the general rule to its exception, or the general one reads as unconditional. That pointer is
  the one sentence a rewrite may add that its source didn't have; name it as an addition when
  you report the change.
- **Ordering the clauses** — the default first, then the `if you can't` fallback, then
  `consider` for an optional aid, then the `don't` that the earlier clauses make unnecessary.
- **Choosing modality** — grade it per clause and claim no more than the rule needs. Keep
  `never` and `always` for the genuinely absolute and reach for `prefer`, `avoid` or `rather
  than` otherwise; escalating a `don't` into a `never` changes the rule rather than rewording
  it.
- **Naming a mechanism** — name the check, helper or skill that owns the mechanics, and stop.
  Its parameters, options and failure modes live with it, and restating them here is a copy
  that goes stale. The exception is a mechanism you are telling the reader to *run*, below.
- **Telling the reader to *run* something** — ship the literal invocation in a fenced block, not
  the file's name. The reader is composing a call rather than looking a mechanism up, so a bare
  filename buys a probe every time — the `--help` that prints nothing, then the `cat`, then a
  hand-built command. (1)
- **Closing a block** — say what the other clauses make unnecessary ("don't also comment the
  duplication — the guard covers it"), so nobody adds belt-and-braces.
- **Keeping an exception** — an exception that changes what the reader would do is part of the
  rule; one that only reassures is padding.
- **Cutting a rule's prose** — drop rationale that only restates the rule, examples that
  re-express it, and mechanics another document owns. Keep the motivation itself: a consequence
  the reader needs in order to apply the rule under pressure earns its clause; rationale the
  reader doesn't need at act time goes to the references doc below.
- **Auditing a file of rules that already exists** — take each rule and ask what a reader would
  get wrong without it. Fold the one whose subject points back at its neighbour; cut the one another
  pack already carries, the one a check now enforces (keeping only the half the check can't see),
  and the one whose mechanism has since been retired — a rule naming code that no longer exists
  teaches a world the reader won't find.
- **Rewriting an existing rule** — carry the source's own strength forward. A rewrite must not
  weaken a rule, and it must not strengthen one either.

## The references doc — where a rule's rationale lives

A pack keeps **one** `references.md` beside its `RULES.md`, servicing all of the pack's prose
files and its checks. It exists for maintenance and review — the periodic pass that asks
whether a rule still earns its place needs the reason it was written — never for daily agentic
work: no rule sends its reader there, and no session loads it. So it stays in the repo that
owns the pack and never vendors: a member mounting a canon pack receives the rules, not the
reasoning behind them, and the pass that reaffirms them runs where the pack lives.

- **Adding a rule that has a rationale** — write the brief rule in `RULES.md` (or the skill),
  and put the reason in `references.md`. End the rule with the bare marker — `… never a
  filesystem walk. (3)` — and nothing else: don't name the references file, don't link it,
  don't ask the reader to follow anything. Not every rule needs one; a rule whose reason is
  self-evident from its consequence clause carries no marker.
- **Writing the entry** — one bullet per entry, keyed by the citing file's own namespace:
  `- **(RULES-3)** <reason>` for a rule in `RULES.md`, `- **(<skill-name>-3)** <reason>` for a
  line in that skill's `SKILL.md`; the marker in the prose file stays the bare `(3)` and
  resolves within its own file's namespace. Write the reason so a future review can **reaffirm
  the rule from it**: what would have to be true for the rule to be retired.
  - A **workaround** explains the issue with not using it, with the evidence (the failing run,
    the error, the measured cost).
  - A **technology guideline** cites the original documentation it derives from.
  - An **owner decision** carries the language of the request that set it.
- **Numbering** — numbers are stable identifiers, not positions: the next entry takes its
  file's next unused number, a removed entry leaves a gap, and nothing ever renumbers (a
  renumber breaks every marker at once). One entry may serve several rules in its file; a rule
  may cite several entries (`(3, 7)`).
- **A check's rationale** — the entry points at the check, since a declaration admits no
  comment and no new key: `- **(check:growth-write-scope)** <reason>`, same reaffirmation
  standard. There is no marker on the check side.
- **Removing a rule or check** — remove its entry in the same change, unless another rule
  still cites it.

The `references-integrity` check holds the mechanism together: every marker must resolve to an
entry in the pack's own `references.md`, and every `check:` entry must name a check the pack
still carries. The `rule-revalidation` task is the mechanism's consumer — it reaffirms
referenced rules and checks against their recorded reasons on its weekly pass.

## Migrating an existing pack onto the references doc

An existing pack — a repo's local pack, or a shared canon pack worked on canon-side (a member
never edits the mounted canon) — migrates opportunistically, one pack per pass, whenever a pass
is already editing it. An unmarked rule stays valid forever, so there is no fleet sweep to
force and no straggler to chase; the check only judges markers that exist.

1. **Create `references.md`** beside the pack's `RULES.md` on its first entry, not before.
2. **Work each rule**: keep the act-time consequence clause inline; move review-only rationale —
   the evidence story, inline issue ids, a cost the reader doesn't need mid-act — into an entry
   and end the rule with its marker. Shrink-only on the rules side: a rule may lose review-only
   rationale in this pass, never gain text.
3. **Recover the missing reasons from history, source-first**: for a rule that states no reason,
   read the commit that added it and that commit's PR and issue *before* re-reading the rule —
   derive the entry from the source, then diff against what the rule implied. The commit
   message, PR body and issue discussion are where this corpus already keeps a rule's evidence.
4. **Never invent an entry.** A rule whose reason can't be recovered stays unmarked — an audit
   or the `rule-revalidation` pass judges whether it still earns its place; a plausible-sounding
   fabricated rationale would let a future review reaffirm a rule on false grounds.
5. **Cover the checks** worth reaffirming with `check:` entries the same way, from their `why`
   text and their adding commit's PR.

## Evidence

The commit and its PR remain the archive — dates, session ids, quoted exchanges and the story
of the incident live there, never in the rule. What the references doc takes from them is only
the **reaffirmable core**: the reason and the minimum evidence a future review needs to re-test
it. Keep a measurement inline in the rule only where the number *is* the argument — a cost the
reader wouldn't believe stated qualitatively.

skills.name: writing-repo-scanning-checks
skills.content:
Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/writing-repo-scanning-checks

# Writing a check that scans the repo

- **Choosing the file set** — take it from `git ls-files` rather than a filesystem walk with
  paths to skip, and remember a brand-new file is untracked until you add it, so a green run
  isn't coverage of it.

- **Scanning for a forbidden token** — strip comments first so it matches code, not prose —
  string-aware, since a `//` inside a URL is not a comment. Reuse `stripComments` from
  [`engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs`](../../../../engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs);
  if the scan can't import it, inline the same pass and point a comment back at that source.
  Strip in **both** directions — a comment that documents or warns about the banned pattern is
  exactly where a naive check trips over its own reasoning, so a commented-out instance must not
  count as present either.

- **Proving the check silent** — run it against the repo's own **real** sources, not only a
  synthetic clean fixture — a fixture spelling the same gap the check has just keeps proving the
  matching, and only a real-tree run can disagree with you.

skills.name: production-retrospective
skills.content:
Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/production-retrospective

# Production retrospective

[verify-in-production](../verify-in-production/SKILL.md) proves a **point assertion**, once:
artifact X reads Y, pass or fail. An element big enough to have a design deserves a second look of
a different kind — not "did it go live" but "did the design survive contact". Once it has worked
*as planned* for about a week, somebody should read its production record and answer four
questions:

1. **Is it working?** Every part of its loop ran and closed — count the strands, the wrong
   closes, the parks, not just the happy paths.
2. **Is it misused?** Do people or neighbouring machinery interact with it against its contract?
3. **Is it overused?** Which uses cost runs or attention and returned nothing — and what should
   the bar exclude?
4. **Is it underused?** What did the design mean to cover that nothing reaches — a trigger that
   never fires, a manual ask that should have been a mechanism?

The four questions are only the frame. What gives them teeth is a brief that already knows what
the element was *supposed* to do — and that knowledge exists exactly once, while the element is
being designed. So this skill has two moments: the brief is **written with the design**, and the
review **runs** a week into production. The reader at either moment must not be the author's
memory: the review is filed as a mechanism that comes back on its own (RULES.md's *When verifying
now is genuinely impossible* names the principle; this skill is its review-shaped sibling).

## When one is owed

The bar: **the element earned a design doc or a phased tracking issue.** A minor feature files no
retrospective — its proof is a test that ran, or verify-in-production's point assertion, and this
skill adds nothing to that. Filing retrospectives for small changes buries the reviews that matter
under reviews with nothing to find.

Two triggers own the filing today:

- **A migration plan's chain.** The retrospective is the chain's **last link**, filed with the
  rest of the chain when the plan is agreed —
  [writing-migration-plans](../writing-migration-plans/SKILL.md) owns the chain's mechanics. It
  rides `Blocked-by:` on the final execution step, so the queue holds it until the migration is
  actually done.
- **A merge that completes a design-doc'd element outside any chain.** File it at the merge,
  beside verify-in-production's own filing moment — the two are separate calls, and a point
  assertion neither requires nor replaces the retrospective.

## The brief is written at design time, not when the retrospective runs

What to retrospect on is a design question, answered while the element is being designed — in the
same pass that writes the design doc, and recorded in the retrospective issue's body (with the
expectations themselves in the design doc, where they are part of the end state). Answered when
the retrospective runs it is too late twice over: the designer's intent has left everyone's head,
and a number nobody thought to record cannot be read back. The brief answers, concretely, for
*this* element:

- **What is expected to happen, and in what amounts.** Volumes and rates, not adjectives: how
  many filings, runs, adoptions, visits per week; which counts should be zero and which would be
  worrying at zero. An expectation without a quantity cannot be missed.
- **What behaviours are expected** — from users and from neighbouring machinery. Who reaches for
  it, when, instead of what; what they were doing before it existed.
- **How each expectation is measured.** The concrete artifact each number is read from — an issue
  count under a label, a run log, a usage file, a stamp, a dashboard — not "we'll see".
- **What would signal misuse** — the interactions its contract forbids, stated so a run can
  recognize them in the record.
- **What would signal overuse** — the cost that would show the bar is too low: filings that find
  nothing, runs that burn sessions to no verdict.
- **What would signal a wrong design decision.** Per decision the design doc records with its
  alternatives: what observation would mean the rejected alternative was right after all.
- **Which decisions are cheap to re-examine.** A default, a cadence, a threshold, a model choice
  can be revisited from evidence; a storage shape or a public contract cannot. Mark the cheap
  ones so the review re-opens them freely and treats the load-bearing ones as expensive claims.
- **Which metrics the review requires, and how the run will access them.** Every measurement
  above must be readable by the unattended run — name the artifact and the read. A metric that
  does not exist yet is an implementation requirement discovered at design time: build the
  counter, the log line, the label with the element itself, or the retrospective arrives with
  nothing to read (the same discipline as RULES.md's *Writing code that can silently do nothing*).

## What you file

One issue on the ad-hoc lane — the same lane and the same first-lines field-block placement
[`/do-later`](../do-later/SKILL.md) files under, with the mark it applies: **`task:origin:ad-hoc`**.
Title `Retrospective: <the element, in a few words>`. Make it a **sub-issue** of the element's
tracking issue (or, with no tracker, of the design's own issue), so the element shows the review
still owed on it.

```
Blocked-by: #<the chain's final execution link>   (chain case)
Not-before: <ISO instant ≈ a week past the merge>  (merge case)
Retry-every: 7 days
Model: opus
```

`Model: opus` because this is judgment work — weighing a record against a design — not the field
read a verification makes. Never `Automerge:` — a retrospective has nothing to merge.

The body is the run's whole brief — the design-time answers above, addressed to a run that will
never see the conversation: the subject (the design doc, the tracking issue), the **record to
read** with each metric's access spelled out, the expected amounts, and the named signals for
misuse, overuse and each re-examinable decision. Then the playbook:

1. **Read when the subject completed** — the final link's close, or the merge — from the artifact
   itself, never inferred from elapsed time. The horizon runs from that instant, not from the
   filing: a chain files its retrospective at plan time, when nobody knows when the migration will
   end. Less than the horizon ago → re-arm exactly as a verification does (`Not-before:` to
   completion + horizon, clear the `task:status:*` label, no comment) and leave the issue open.
2. **Ripe → review.** Re-read what the design *promises* — the brief's expectations and signals,
   and the design doc behind them — **before reading the record**, then diff the record against it
   — RULES.md's *Correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source*, applied to
   behaviour. Answer the four questions with the brief's own measurements: counts and links, not
   impressions.
3. **Findings become issues — one issue per systemic fault, and the run fixes nothing — routed by
   kind.** An **implementation fault** — the element does not do what the design says — is a bug:
   file it as an actionable task issue the queue can implement. A **design fault** — the element
   does what the design says and the record shows that decision was wrong — is nobody's to fix
   silently: file it as a **discussion issue** carrying the evidence and the design doc's own
   alternatives, parked so it waits on the **owner's decision** (the park lever the repo's queue
   provides, or a plain ask to the owner where it has none). Comment the summary on this issue
   linking each finding, and close it as completed. Four clean answers are also a result: close
   with the summary saying so.
4. **A record the run cannot read** — an artifact behind a scope or egress wall — **parks for a
   human naming exactly which read failed.** A blocked read answers "all clean" exactly the way a
   healthy mechanism does; never convert one into a verdict.

## The lane is open: defining another retrospective class

The design retrospective above is one **class** of a general shape. A class is four things: a
**trigger** (the event that files it — an event, never a habit), a **subject and its record** (what
to read), a **horizon** (how long the subject must live before judging), and a **brief** (the
questions, usually these four re-aimed). Anyone may define another, at the scope that owns the
recurring moment:

- **A canon pack** whose territory has its own "lived long enough to judge" moment declares a
  class in its own prose or skills, routed through the growth lifecycle like any promotion.
- **A repo's local pack** defines classes for subjects only that repo has.
- **The fleet enforcer** files fleet-wide ones, where the subject spans members.

Classes worth proposing when their trigger next fires — each a proposal to its owning pack, not a
rule this skill sets:

| Class | Trigger | The brief asks |
|---|---|---|
| Post-adoption | a repo adopts Claudinite or a pack | did its tasks run, did checks stay green, did the owner fight it |
| New scheduled task | a new task's first week of runs | is the cadence right, do runs converge, is it filing noise |
| Fleet rollout | a fleet-baseline force, or a pack seeded across members | did every member converge, what parked, what stayed `unknown` |
| Rule effectiveness | a growth-extract batch lands | did the friction recur, are the rules loaded but ignored |
| Grant of a credential or permission | a token created or widened | is it used at all, is it still least-privilege |
| Retirement | a mechanism removed or a repo handed off | do references dangle, did anything break silently |

## Then say what you filed

One line back to the owner: the issue link, what it waits on, and the horizon.
